reasoning.bridgeProposition: Deep forward propagation can be interpreted as a discretization of an ordinary differential equation (ODE), and the stability of this propagation—which determines whether gradients explode or vanish—depends on the smoothness of network parameters across layers (i.e., small time derivatives) and on the spectral properties of the layer-wise transformation matrices. Penalizing the time derivative of parameters enforces this smoothness and yields a well-posed learning problem for arbitrarily deep networks.
reasoning.paperBObservation: In a neural architecture search framework using additive regularization, a penalty that discourages large changes in weight values between adjacent layers is employed. The resulting regularized models are observed to be significantly more stable and to converge to less structurally complex yet more accurate solutions compared with non-regularized models.

It derives that stability requires the real parts of Jacobian eigenvalues to be near zero and, crucially, that the time derivatives of propagation weights must be small (smooth dynamics). It therefore proposes derivative-based regularization to favor smooth time dynamics.
reasoning.step2: Paper B employs an additive regularization schedule for neural architecture search that includes a penalty on local differences in weight values between adjacent layers, which is a discrete version of a time-derivative penalty. Its experiments show that regularized models are more stable and achieve better accuracy with lower complexity. Applying Paper A's proposition, this penalty enforces the smooth parameter trajectories required for stable ODE integration, which prevents gradient instabilities and allows reliable pruning of deep architectures.

Paper A supplies the ODE interpretation and the specific smoothness condition required for stable forward propagation. Without Paper A, one cannot explain why penalizing local weight differences across layers should stabilize deep training; without Paper B, the condition remains abstract and is not tied to a concrete neural architecture search experiment and design choice.

answerWithPaperReferences: Paper A interprets deep forward propagation as a discretization of an ordinary differential equation (ODE) and demonstrates that the exploding or vanishing gradient phenomenon corresponds to instability in this underlying ODE [Paper A]. It establishes that stable forward propagation requires the network parameters to vary smoothly across layers—i.e., their time derivatives must be small—and that the Jacobian eigenvalues of the layer-wise transformations should have real parts near zero [Paper A]. To achieve this, Paper A proposes derivative-based regularization that penalizes rapid changes in propagation weights over depth [Paper A]. Paper B proposes an additive regularization schedule for neural architecture search that includes a penalty on local differences in weight values between adjacent layers, which serves as a discrete analogue of a time-derivative penalty [Paper B]. In computational experiments, Paper B observes that models trained with such regularization are significantly more stable and converge to structures of lower complexity while maintaining or improving accuracy [Paper B]. By combining these findings, the local-difference penalty enforces the smooth parameter dynamics required for stable ODE integration; this prevents gradient instabilities during training, which in turn allows the architecture search to reliably prune redundant neurons and optimize a compact, accurate network.
answerWithoutPaperReferences: Deep forward propagation in very deep networks can be viewed as a discretized ordinary differential equation, and its stability depends critically on the smoothness of network parameters across layers. If the weights change too rapidly from one layer to the next, the forward propagation becomes unstable, producing exploding or vanishing gradients that render training ill-posed. An additive regularization schedule that penalizes large changes in weight values between adjacent layers enforces smooth parameter trajectories, which is precisely the condition needed for stable ODE integration. By satisfying this stability condition, the training process remains well-posed even for deep architectures, enabling the optimization procedure to successfully prune redundant neurons and reduce structural complexity without sacrificing predictive accuracy.
isNotSingleHop: Paper A alone presents the ODE interpretation and the smoothness condition for stable forward propagation, but it does not discuss additive regularization schedules, local-difference penalties, or neural architecture search experiments. Paper B alone reports that regularized models are more stable and can be pruned to lower complexity, yet it does not provide the theoretical mechanism explaining why penalizing local weight differences across layers should prevent gradient instabilities in deep networks. Answering the question requires applying Paper A's theoretical stability condition to interpret Paper B's empirical observation and design choice, which is impossible from either paper in isolation. The reasoning is not entity linking because it does not merely identify the same regularization term in both papers; instead, it uses Paper A's dynamical-system analysis to explain the causal effect of Paper B's penalty.

First 15118 characters: Stable Architectures for Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Deep neural networks have become invaluable tools for supervised machine learning, e.g., classification of text or images. While often offering superior results over traditional techniques and successfully expressing complicated patterns in data, deep architectures are known to be challenging to design and train such that they generalize well to new data. Important issues with deep architectures are numerical instabilities in derivative-based learning algorithms commonly called exploding or vanishing gradients. In this paper we propose new forward propagation techniques inspired by systems of Ordinary Differential Equations (ODE) that overcome this challenge and lead to well-posed learning problems for arbitrarily deep networks. The backbone of our approach is our interpretation of deep learning as a parameter estimation problem of nonlinear dynamical systems. Given this formulation, we analyze stability and well-posedness of deep learning and use this new understanding to develop new network architectures. We relate the exploding and vanishing gradient phenomenon to the stability of the discrete ODE and present several strategies for stabilizing deep learning for very deep networks. While our new architectures restrict the solution space, several numerical experiments show their competitiveness with state-of-the-art networks.
Introduction: In this work, we propose new architectures for Deep Neural Networks (DNN) and exemplarily show their effectiveness for solving supervised Machine Learning (ML) problems; for a general overview about DNN and ML see, e.g., , , , and reference therein. We consider the following classification problem: Assume we are given training data consisting of {{formula:3dd5c701-858d-4edf-88bb-4b35618f5869}} feature vectors, {{formula:3a9310e4-4aac-4840-a996-60f8f33ea567}} , and label vectors, {{formula:dbfe280a-7237-4e77-9b2e-fdfd6d8866f4}} , whose {{formula:b906e8e2-59e5-4686-87a1-d957f318b416}} th components represent the likelihood of an example belonging to class {{formula:44933d76-9b00-4dff-8557-f3111adc0102}} . The goal is to learn a function that approximates the data-label relation on the training data and generalizes well to similar unlabeled data. Our goals in this work are to highlight the relation of the learning problem to dynamic inverse problems, analyze its stability and ill-posedness for commonly used architectures, and derive new architectures that alleviate some of these difficulties for arbitrarily deep architectures.We are particularly interested in deep learning, i.e., machine learning using neural networks with many hidden layers. DNNs have been successful in supervised learning, particularly when the relationship between the data and the labels is highly nonlinear; see, e.g., , , , and reference therein. Their depths (i.e., their number of layers) allow DNNs to express complex data-label relationships since each layer nonlinearly transforms the features and therefore effectively filters the information content.Given the training data {{formula:cae15ccb-38cc-4d41-990a-7242b339e97f}} , an inverse problem needs to be solved in order to train a given network architecture. This problem, also called the learning problem, aims at finding a parameterization of the DNN that explains the data-label relation and generalizes well to new unlabeled data. Clearly, using deeper network architectures increases the capacity of the network but also the dimensionality, and thus the computational complexity, of the parameter estimation problem. Additionally, more labeled data is required to calibrate very deep networks reliably. Therefore, despite the fact that neural networks have been used since the early 70's, deep learning has only recently revolutionized many applications fueled by advances in computational hardware and availability of massive data sets.Well-known sources of difficulty in deep learning are the dimensionality and non-convexity of the associated optimization problem. Traditionally, stochastic gradient descent methods have been used . It has been observed that the performance of the DNN can be highly dependent on the choice of optimization algorithm and sample size , . Furthermore, it has been noted that some optimization algorithms yield DNNs that generalize poorly to new unlabeled data .Additional difficulties in deep learning stem from instabilities of the underlying forward model, most importantly, the propagation of features through the DNN. As has been shown in , the output of some networks can be unstable with respect to small perturbations in the original features. A related problem is the observation of vanishing or exploding gradients . These results are unsettling since predictions made by networks with unstable forward propagation are very sensitive to small perturbations of the input features (as is common, e.g., in adversarial attacks), which may render the network useless in practice.The main goal of this work is to gain new insight into the stability of the forward propagation and the well-posedness of the learning problem summarized in the following two questions:Given a network architecture and parameters obtained by some optimization process, is the forward propagation problem well-posed? Is the learning problem well-posed? In other words, given sufficient training are there parameters such that the DNN generalizes well or can generalization be improved by adding appropriate regularization?The first question is important because, while it may be possible to fit the training data even for unstable forward propagation models, the trained network is unlikely to generalize. In other words, small deviations in the data, e.g., due to noise, may be drastically amplified by the forward propagation, resulting in incorrect labels. We show that the forward problem can be thought of as a discretization of an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE). Therefore, the stability of the network corresponds to the stability of its underlying ODE. Based on this observation we develop stability criteria for a simplified version of the commonly used Residual Network (ResNet) architecture and develop new network architectures that are ensured to be stable and lead to well-posed learning problems.The paper is organized as follows. In Section we give a brief mathematical derivation of the deep learning problem illustrated using the ResNet architecture. In Section we analyze the stability of the simplified ResNet forward propagation and the well-posedness of the resulting learning problem. Our analysis and examples suggest stability criteria, and as a result, in Section , we propose three new stable architectures. In Section we propose regularization functions favoring smoothness of parameters and multi-level ideas to initialize deep networks. In Section we demonstrate the effectiveness of our new architectures on a number of small-scale model problems and explore their effectiveness for solving image classification problems. Finally, in Section we summarize the paper.
Mathematical Formulation of the Deep Learning Problem: In this section we briefly describe three main ingredients of deep learning relevant to our work; for a comprehensive introduction see, e.g., , , , . First, we outline forward propagation techniques, which transforms the input features in a nonlinear way to filter their information. Second, we describe classification, which predicts the class label probabilities using the features at the output layer (i.e., the output of the forward propagation). Finally, we formulate the learning problem, which aims at estimating parameters of the forward propagation and classification that approximate the data-label relation.For notational convenience we stack the training features and labels row-wise into matrices {{formula:80f86ec0-0883-441a-926d-a1234bf61e12}} and {{formula:c7a76343-b06d-43fd-a6a8-793ff3ad5852}} .To exemplify our discussion of forward propagation we consider a simplified version of the Residual Neural Network (ResNet) model that has been very successful in classifying images using deep network architectures; see for other options. In ResNets, the forward propagation of the input values, {{formula:0befe704-07e6-46ff-8a7b-39a49c96deb8}} , through a network consisting of {{formula:453f3a0f-d91a-4632-80db-2ad1e4f1119a}} layers is given by {{formula:36dbca77-4a54-4025-ba44-5f4b2bcfb15c}}The propagation in Eq. REF is parametrized by the nonlinear activation function {{formula:dee7e9e1-7235-45fe-9ca2-1c59c2bd27da}} and affine transformations represented by their weights, {{formula:bb904d74-1790-45ab-bdb7-d1ff8fe12e34}} , and biases, {{formula:9b5f461b-acfd-4f1a-a5c5-9436406c5a05}} . We augmented the original formulation in by the parameter {{formula:3bea606e-47ab-470f-b0e0-58c24ba69140}} in order to increase the stability of the forward propagation and allow for a continuous interpretation of the process; see also Section . The values {{formula:1a41ff2a-8ebb-4849-a6ed-b4524ad4b197}} are also called hidden layers and {{formula:a4b61ee5-315b-4d9a-9af8-54355c14dcaa}} is called the output layer. The activation function is applied element-wise and is typically (piecewise) smooth and monotonically non-decreasing. As two commonly used examples, we consider the hyperbolic tangent and the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activations {{formula:2436dddf-3d29-49d7-bf43-334ce72db05d}}The class label probabilities are predicted using the values at the output layers, {{formula:7453947e-dcb4-41f3-b355-c3f39a58298c}} , a hypothesis function {{formula:f72ff03d-3227-4854-8044-ce3e7d59064c}} , and its associated weights, {{formula:4c83b3b4-f7f3-4233-adff-3d37037b7629}} , and bias, {{formula:9fb5b6d5-3194-4bd0-a93f-494292395854}} . Here {{formula:53e4c10b-b0f8-43e8-a615-c5bc2268df5f}} denotes the {{formula:8661df40-f817-4e44-8924-4b306b55132a}} -dimensional vector of all ones. For Bernoulli variables (i.e., {{formula:8d6c85c5-55e6-4c1b-af3f-0547ec4aedfd}} ) it is natural to consider the logistic regression function {{formula:8eda0da3-4662-4007-a8f1-307a43adc5d0}}where the exponential and the division are applied element-wise. For Multinomial distributions we use the softmax function {{formula:21a34460-107f-4908-b1f5-b32a2ed7f6cd}}The learning problem aims at estimating the parameters of the forward propagation (i.e., {{formula:2ee1536e-fbe0-406b-95b9-d302e555837e}} and {{formula:47cdab05-2e8c-4dd2-92c0-7452e7951fe4}} ) and the classifier ({{formula:10a7e735-1af3-44b0-8e8b-767021746a32}} and {{formula:68da0de3-28d0-44a5-b769-220eb58234bc}} ) so that the DNN accurately approximates the data-label relation for the training data and generalizes to new unlabeled data. As we show below, the learning problem can be cast as a dynamic inverse problem, which provides new opportunities for applying theoretical and computational techniques from parameter estimation to deep learning problems. We phrase learning as an optimization problem {{formula:8bd7dda8-4b82-431d-92ed-5dc4cdd98934}}where the loss function {{formula:3260f515-3c3d-4fe2-bf1b-23bbb5b52011}} is convex in its first argument and measures the quality of the predicted class label probabilities, the convex regularizer {{formula:a604e638-4017-4860-a521-356505d7b4dd}} penalizes undesirable (e.g., highly oscillatory) parameters, and the parameter {{formula:a9e7d8e2-4532-41f9-8dbc-e460442bb008}} balances between minimizing the data fit and regularity of the parameters. A simple example for a loss function is the sum-of-squared difference function {{formula:aadd893e-fa21-4883-9445-eeb4d9638663}} . Since our numerical experiments deal with classification we use cross entropy loss functions. Choosing an "optimal" regularizer, {{formula:2995f6b7-d372-4dc2-bd1f-907055eebb0f}} , and regularization parameter, {{formula:3809d805-6fef-4004-8d5a-956cd9f70103}} , is both crucial and nontrivial. Commonly Tikhonov regularization , , , also referred to as weight decay, has been used , although, other possibilities enforcing sparsity or other structure have been proposed . We introduce novel regularization functions in Section . For simplicity, we assume that a suitable value of {{formula:a953b19e-bb53-4a3d-ab3d-f5acae251250}} is chosen by the user or that it is done dynamically as suggested in .There are numerous approaches to solving the learning problem. In this work we use a simple block coordinate descent method to demonstrate the properties of the forward propagation. Our method alternates between updating the parameters of the classifier {{formula:702d82fa-6061-429b-97c7-0cb543aad8c7}} fixing the current value of the propagated features {{formula:0ff6bb71-3a25-40f9-a4f7-cfa80ceed43f}} and then updating the parameters of the forward propagation while keeping the updated weights of the classifier fixed. The first problem is typically convex and the latter problem is generally non-convex due to the forward propagation process. Both steps are based on subsampling the training data. To this end note that most common loss functions can be written as a sum over all examples, i.e., {{formula:075ea705-d043-4009-9fa7-a96561f63804}}where {{formula:1d63eb36-08dc-475b-9a7e-fd58cb2fa4c6}} is a randomly chosen set updated in each iteration of the block coordinate descent method. The size of the batches is a parameter in our algorithm whose choice depends on the size and complexity of the problem and resource considerations. In the following, we assume the sample size is constant; for adaptive selection of sample size see, e.g., . In each iteration of the block coordinate descent scheme, our algorithm approximately solves the resulting classification problem using an Newton-PCG method, i.e., an inexact Newton method that uses a Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (PCG) method to determine a search direction (see, e.g., , , ). Subsequently, the weights of the forward propagation are updated using a Gauss-Newton-PCG method. Note that gradient and approximated Hessian computations require matrix-vector products with the derivative matrices of the values of the output layer, {{formula:79762c83-8d98-4149-bf8f-2ac32f095ed0}} , with respect to {{formula:98e6d564-b9c9-4353-a857-bc160031dc05}} and {{formula:57e1b3c8-cb43-4cc7-bb83-c6a17d69e723}} . The matrix-vector products with the derivative matrix can be computed without its explicit construction through forward and backward propagation, respectively; see also . However, this requires storing (or recomputing) the values at the output layers; see, for instance, Section REF for derivative computation. Therefore, as also suggested in , we subsample {{formula:9271e52a-1035-4bf6-a699-bb0e6a1af5a6}} further to reduce the cost of the Hessian matrix-vector products in our PCG scheme.Our implementation includes computing the validation error in each iteration of the block coordinate descent method. The final output of our algorithm are the parameters that achieve the lowest validation error.

Summary and conclusions: In this paper, we expose the relation between deep learning and dynamic inverse problems and lay the foundation for fruitful research at the interface of inverse problems and data science. Specifically, we propose new architectures for deep neural networks (DNN) that improve the stability of the forward propagation. Using derivative-based regularization, we also improve the well-posedness of the learning task. We also propose a multi-level strategy that simplifies the choice of initial parameters and thereby simplifies the training of very deep networks. Our forward propagation methods are inspired by Hamiltonian systems and motivated by a stability analysis that is based on a continuous formulation of the learning problem.Our stability discussion in Section provides new insights why ResNets , a commonly used forward propagation scheme in deep learning, can be unstable. Our result is based on a continuous interpretation of a simplified version of ResNets as a system of nonlinear ODEs and a standard stability argument. Using intuitive examples, we show the impact of the spectral properties of the transformation matrices on the stability of the forward propagation and state conditions under which gradients explode, vanish, or are stable. We also note that stability depends on the smoothness of the network parameters over time. Based on our findings and numerical experience, we argue that it is desirable to restrict ResNets to matrices that lead to Jacobians whose real parts of the spectrum are close to zero and penalize the time-derivative of network parameters through regularization. We also emphasize that the well-posedness of the learning problem in ResNets relies on sufficiently small time steps. Extending our analysis to more general versions of ResNet is straightforward and will be investigated in future work.Motivated by our theoretical considerations, we propose three new forward propagation methods in Section that can be used to obtain well-posed learning problems for arbitrarily deep networks. The first one is a simple modification of ResNet that applies a linear transformation to the transformation matrices to annihilate the real parts of their eigenvalues. The other two methods are inspired by Hamiltonian systems and provide alternative ways to preserve in information in the forward propagation. The Hamiltonian networks require special integration techniques; see for details on their treatment. The second-order forward propagation can be discretized using the leapfrog method, and our implementation of the first-order propagation uses the Verlet method. While the stability of the leapfrog method requires matrices with non-positive real eigenvalues, the Verlet method does not require any restrictions and yields the best performance in our numerical experiments.Our approach to stabilizing the learning problem for very deep architectures differs significantly from existing approaches, most importantly batch normalization . Batch normalization scales values at hidden layers to prevent vanishing or exploding gradients and has been shown to improve the efficiency of training deep networks. In contrast to that our approach does not modify the values of the features, but alleviates the need of normalization by constructing stable forward propagation methods.In order to improve the generalization quality, improve stability, and simplify training of deep networks we also propose new regularization approaches that depend on our continuous formulation of the problem. We use derivative-based regularizers to favor smooth time dynamics and, for image classification problems, spatially smooth classification weights. To further regularize and simplify the initialization of the learning algorithm, we employ a multi-level learning strategy that gradually increases the depth of the network. In our experiments, this approach has been a simple yet effective way to obtain good initializations for the learning problems. Our regularization methods are commonly used in imaging science, e.g., image registration , however, to the best of our knowledge not commonly employed in deep learning. Our numerical examples show that approximately solving the regularized learning problem yields works that generalize well even when the number of network parameters exceeds the number of training features.We illustrate our methods using three academic test problems with available ground-truth and the MNIST problem , which is a commonly used benchmark problem for image classification. Our experiments show that the proposed new architectures yield results that are competitive with the established ResNet architecture. This is particularly noteworthy for the proposed anti-symmetric ResNet, where we restrict the dimensionality of the search space to ensure stability.By establishing a link between deep learning and dynamic inverse problems, we are positive that this work will stimulate further research by both communities. An important item of future work is investigating the impact of the proposed architectures on the performance of learning algorithms. Currently, stochastic gradient descent is commonly used to train deep neural networks due to its computational efficiency and empirical evidence supporting its generalizations . A specific question is if the improvements in the forward propagation and regularization proposed in this paper will lead to better generalization properties of subsampled second-order methods such as , . Another thrust of future work is the development of automatic parameter selection strategies for deep learning based on the approaches presented, e.g., in , , , , . A particular challenge in this application is the nontrivial relationship between the regularization parameters chosen for the classification and forward propagation parameters.

questionDraft: The ARGOS survey finds that its most metal-rich bulge giants near the Galactic plane deviate systematically from theoretical isochrones. What specific limitations in the construction of the Schlegel, Finkbeiner & Davis reddening map explain why an overestimation of reddening in high-extinction regions would cause such isochrone deviations, and how does this affect the derived stellar temperatures?
question: Why do the most metal-rich giant stars in the inner Galactic bulge, when dereddened using the Schlegel, Finkbeiner & Davis all-sky reddening map, show the largest deviations from theoretical isochrones toward higher temperatures, and what specific limitations in that map’s construction are responsible for this artifact in regions of high visual extinction?
answerWithPaperReferences: [Paper A] demonstrates that the SFD all-sky reddening map overestimates reddening by a factor of 1.3–1.5 in regions with smooth extinction A_V > 0.5 mag. This bias arises because the map’s conversion from dust column density to reddening is calibrated using the colors and Mg II line strengths of 389 elliptical galaxies, 90% of which have E(B-V) < 0.1, so the relation is poorly constrained at high opacity. In addition, the dust color temperature map employed by SFD is limited by DIRBE’s ~1.4° spatial resolution, which smears temperature gradients and reduces effective resolution near steep extinction peaks. [Paper B] finds that in the ARGOS survey, the most metal-rich bulge giants—located in the highest-reddening fields closest to the Galactic plane—deviate most strongly from BaSTI isochrones, appearing shifted toward higher temperatures and lower gravities. By combining the two results, the isochrone mismatch is explained as a consequence of the SFD map’s systematic overestimation of reddening in these high-extinction fields: applying too large a reddening correction makes the dereddened stellar colors too blue, which drives the spectroscopic temperature scale upward and displaces the stars from the true isochrones in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.
answerWithoutPaperReferences: The systematic offset of metal-rich bulge giants from theoretical isochrones is caused by the adopted all-sky reddening map overestimating interstellar extinction in high-opacity regions. The map’s empirical conversion from dust emission to reddening was calibrated using elliptical galaxies that almost all lie in low-reddening environments, so the relation becomes inaccurate where visual extinction exceeds about half a magnitude. Furthermore, the temperature map used in its construction has a spatial resolution of only about 1.4 degrees, which blurs small-scale temperature structure and exacerbates errors in high-extinction areas. When this overestimated reddening is used to correct the observed colors of bulge stars near the Galactic plane, the dereddened colors are too blue, leading to erroneously high stellar temperatures and altered surface gravities that shift the stars away from the true stellar evolution models.
isNotSingleHop: Paper A alone describes the SFD map’s calibration bias and resolution limitations but does not discuss stellar isochrones, spectroscopic surveys, or bulge stellar populations. Paper B alone notes that Schlegel reddening may be too high by 30–50% in high-extinction regions and that this could contribute to isochrone deviations, but it presents reddening as only one of three possible explanations alongside stellar models and temperature calibration, and it does not explain the physical or instrumental origin of the overestimation. Therefore, neither paper in isolation can answer why the specific construction limitations of the SFD map cause isochrone deviations for metal-rich bulge giants. The question requires applying Paper A’s mechanistic proposition about the map’s failure modes to interpret Paper B’s observational result, rather than simply identifying the SFD map as a named artifact or matching the numerical overestimation factor.
bridgeEvidencePaperText:
Measuring Galactic Extinction: A Test
abstract: We test the recently published all-sky reddening map of Schlegel, Finkbeiner & Davis (1998 [SFD]) using the extinction study of a region in the Taurus dark cloud complex by Arce & Goodman (1999 [AG]). In their study, AG use four different techniques to measure the amount and structure of the extinction toward Taurus, and all four techniques agree very well. Thus we believe that the AG results are a truthful representation of the extinction in the region and can be used to test the reliability of the SFD reddening map. The results of our test show that the SFD all-sky reddening map, which is based on data from COBE/DIRBE and IRAS/ISSA, overestimates the reddening by a factor of 1.3 to 1.5 in regions of smooth extinction with A_V > 0.5 mag. In some regions of steep extinction gradients the SFD map underestimates the reddening value, probably due to its low spatial resolution. We expect that the astronomical community will be using the SFD reddening map extensively. We offer this Letter as a cautionary note about using the SFD map in regions of high extinction (A_V > 0.5 mag), as it might not be giving accurate reddening values there.
Introduction: Extinction and reddening caused by interstellar dust effects the detected emission from most astronomical sources in the sky. In most galactic and extragalactic studies, especially when studying so called “standard candles,” the effects of dust on the source's detected brightness and color need to be taken into account. Hence it is very desirable to know the extinction (and reddening) anywhere on the sky.Recently Schlegel, Finkbeiner and Davis (1998; hereafter SFD) published an all-sky reddening map, based on satellite observations of far-infrared emission (at 100 and 240 ) from dust. This new reddening map will surely be used by many researchers seeking to apply reddening “corrections” for their work, so it is very important to verify its accuracy and reliability. The SFD map uses data obtained by the DIRBE (Diffuse InfraRed Background Experiment) on board COBE combined with ISSA (IRAS Sky Survey Atlas) images. The COBE/DIRBE experiment had better control of absolute calibration than did IRAS, but a larger beam (0.7; as compared with {{formula:d22fbda7-abf6-41cb-9fc7-1f7465037e7b}} 5 for IRAS). SFD use the DIRBE data to calibrate the IRAS/ISSA images, and, after sophisticated processing, they obtain a full sky map of the 100 emission from dust, with point sources and the zodiacal light foreground removed.See SFD for a full description of their elaborate foreground zodiacal light subtraction technique, point source extraction and overall data reduction. Their resulting reddening map is more accurate and has better resolution ({{formula:7733b5ce-e65a-47d3-ab48-8bdb50beff08}} 6.1) than the previous existing all sky reddening map of Burstein and Heiles (1978, 1982).In order to test the extinction map derived from the SFD analysis, we compare it with Arce & Goodman's (1999; hereafter AG) recent extinction study of a region of the Taurus dark cloud complex. The AG study uses four different techniques to measure extinction along two constant-Right Ascension “cuts” of several degrees in length. The four techniques in AG utilize: 1) the color excess of background stars for which spectral types are known; 2) the ISSA 60 and 100 images; 3) star counts; and 4) an optical ({{formula:d6746e38-6f21-4fae-9710-9de5af007d01}} and {{formula:328ab876-8a9a-430f-83ea-1dbf57b30a75}} ) version of the average color excess method used by Lada et al. (1994). The study finds that all four methods give generally similar results, and concludes that all four techniques are reliable ways to measure extinction in regions where {{formula:6578bf3f-4640-4ae4-aa50-c6f00a7d8b7b}} mag. In this Letter we compare the extinction map derived from SFD to the AG extinction map which is based on ISSA 60 and 100 images in the Taurus region. This comparison provides a test of the reliability of the SFD reddening map for regions of extinction ({{formula:36d4f953-b2a8-4532-897b-3c1a42fa559a}} ) higher than 0.5 mag.
Comparing the two results: In this section we compare the extinction derived from the SFD reddening map (hereafter {{formula:1860b361-c7d1-46bd-a55a-367a51939054}} ) to the extinction AG obtained using the ISSA 60 and 100 maps (hereafter {{formula:e47c0051-b397-4a6f-b801-df2474a3f7ab}} ). In order to be consistent, we must compare both methods with the same spatial resolution. As part of their image reduction procedure, SFD convolve the ISSA images with a FWHM=3.2 Gaussian, which results in ISSA images with 6.1 resolution. For the purpose of comparing the two extinction maps, we also convolve the AG ISSA images with a FWHM=3.2 Gaussian, so that both extinction determinations have the same resolution.When AG compare {{formula:b20ff2e3-4a68-42f4-8205-c1b1164743b0}} with the extinction measured with star counting techniques and the average color excess method (techniques 3 and 4 above), they do so by plotting extinction versus declination. The extinction values shown in Figures 3 and 5 of AG are actually traces of the extinction averaged over the {{formula:ee7f9c44-63bc-4c31-9b07-f7fee4a502bd}} 10 span (in the R.A. direction) of their CCD fields. For consistency we consider the same kind of average, and we obtain the SFD reddening ({{formula:1b94578e-3833-47a0-a4e5-05ac787fc8da}} ) for the two 10 wide constant–R.A. cuts of AG and average {{formula:0cf0ab67-182a-4728-a0c1-cba9b0c93f7c}} over Right Ascension. In order to convert from the color excess value given by the SFD maps to visual extinction, we use the equation {{formula:9994f79f-2745-44d8-bc82-88210aca4457}} , where {{formula:7738b4d5-102b-4dca-8d64-5277903723af}} , the ratio of total-to-selective extinction, is equal to 3.1 (SFD; Kenyon et al. 1994; Vrba & Rydgren 1985).In Figure 1 we plot extinction versus declination for the two constant R.A. cuts in the Taurus dark cloud complex region. In addition to {{formula:f4c3297e-cbf3-493a-a399-c4cceab59fcb}} and {{formula:12106f30-9a3e-47c9-8f57-9217be7d2fd7}} , we show the extinction traces of the extinction obtained from the average color excess and star count methods of AG, for reference. We will concetrate our discussion on the ISSA (AG) and SFD methods. It can be seen that these two methods trace similar structure in both cuts. The extinction peaks associated with the IRAS core Tau M1 (Wood et al. 1994), the dark cloud L1506, the dark cloud B216-217, and the IRAS cores Tau B5 and Tau B11 (Wood et al. 1994) are easily detected. The 1 {{formula:1272ff61-316d-4360-b75b-923cb799d835}} error (not including systematics) of {{formula:93d05d39-01ba-49e6-97d4-5d4983885d86}} is 0.12 mag (AG). SFD quote an uncertainty of 16% in their reddening estimates. For the most part, in regions unassociated with a pronounced peak in extinction, {{formula:9a4f1a76-ec1d-4e4e-8ad0-30b1f7749b73}} is about a factor of 1.3 to 1.5 larger than {{formula:b8a1bb38-46a1-4f5d-8f98-1611baf6c677}} . It is also important to note that in regions where there is a peak in the extinction, the value of {{formula:1f103777-4726-41b5-923d-bc28dec76db2}} is closer to that of {{formula:94b466b8-6647-49ca-bdf3-ddcd57f77d27}} than in the rest of the trace, and in some of the peaks {{formula:d8901d74-64e7-4ea9-aa97-0a4ccbb6740e}} exceeds {{formula:2fd901dd-dc61-4210-8e2f-fc698c00ceac}} .There are two places where the two traces appear to show very different extinction structures. In both of these places {{formula:f434810d-049d-4d5b-b9f8-8b2c4d66f2fe}} shows a steep dip: one is near the peak associated with B216-217 in cut 2 (around declination 26.9); and the other is near the end of the cut, around declination 28.3 (see Figure 1). These two regions coincide with the position of IRAS point sources, and will be discussed in more detail further on.
Comparison between the two methods: SFD use data from the IRAS and DIRBE experiments to construct a full-sky map of the Galactic dust based on its far-infrared emission. The IRAS data are used as a source of 100 flux images, and the DIRBE data are used for absolute calibration and as a source of 240 data. SFD derive the dust color temperature using the ratio of 100 to 240 emission from DIRBENote that deriving dust temperature from a long wavelength color ratio, such as 100/240 is superior to using the 60/100 ratio, because the effects of both point sources and transient heating of small grains are minimized., and then use this dust color temperature to convert their ISSA-based maps of 100 emission to maps of dust column density. As a result of this procedure, the SFD ISSA-based 100 emission map has a spatial resolution of 6.1, but their dust color temperature map has a resolution of {{formula:82769154-cf8a-4886-ad6e-33e60dabc8b5}} 1.4 (Schlegel 1998).To transform from the map proportional to dust column (hereafter {{formula:ca996217-73e9-42cf-aaec-6debb4183a39}} ) to a reddening ({{formula:cbeabf17-4bc5-44b7-9acc-d90c1bcf81b1}} ) map, SFD use the correlation between the intrinsic color of elliptical galaxies and the Mg{{formula:34a1229b-eeaa-481f-93bc-d630cc7e2f20}} line strength. The Mg{{formula:10722ea8-0a95-4af6-b037-992ec1999748}} line strength of an elliptical galaxy correlates well with its intrinsic color so that the Mg{{formula:3eee8240-4a74-4e56-9df5-f365f2f9c4ed}} line index can be used along with photometric measurements of the galaxy in order to obtain a reasonably accurate measurement of its reddening (Faber et al. 1989). SFD use a procedure where the residual of the color versus the Mg{{formula:d75dc4d9-f266-4b0e-a2e4-2547d728ff27}} line index for 389 elliptical galaxies is correlated with the estimated reddening from their maps, using a Spearman Rank method. The resultant fit is then used by SFD to convert from {{formula:2e83ed5f-dc3a-445b-9781-e5e01953d283}} to reddening ({{formula:f6aaee10-5ed8-4def-bcfd-3c035e467f60}} ) at each pixel. We then convert reddening to extinction, using the relation {{formula:d52261a8-ce68-4317-aed0-2e1de810f7aa}} , with {{formula:4353efc8-57e9-4efe-a559-552101144e87}} (SFD).In order to obtain their ISSA-based extinction, {{formula:55d77a17-ea87-429f-84d9-ed3854e6173d}} , AG begin by using ISSA 60 and 100 images to obtain a dust color temperature map from the flux ratio at each pixel. This color temperature is then used to convert the observed 100 flux to 100 optical depth, {{formula:b2f8ed20-6e8b-41c2-808c-29c64a447167}} . As in SFD, the next conversion, from dust opacity to extinction, is tied to a separate technique of obtaining extinction. AG chose to use a method similar to that described in Wood et al. (1994), which itself is ultimately based on work by Jarrett et al. (1989). Jarrett et al. (1989) correlate 60 optical depth ({{formula:7b1d0edd-17b9-416f-b4fd-84cb164c8983}} ) with extinction ({{formula:ebba58c3-09e3-4af1-83e1-580030862cbc}} ) obtained from star counts, and Wood et al. (1994) multiply the Jarrett et al. {{formula:de2ce604-d288-480d-b050-16a7d552f311}} values by 100/60 to derive a conversion from {{formula:787666b4-c63c-42ab-9151-52ef2674945c}} to {{formula:1b3ababf-6ef3-45a2-976d-57f86294986d}} , assuming low optical depth. Thus, using Wood et al.'s technique, AG's conversion of {{formula:cc09b29f-3503-42e4-a870-2b6196e8dee3}} to {{formula:444cb6b1-508b-4433-a90e-de0124ac04da}} ultimately rests on Jarrett et al.'s correlation of 60 optical depth with star counts. As described in AG, this {{formula:2ddc3274-7a49-4c9e-8af4-6b9eb6bf5f5b}} correlation is very tight for {{formula:7d7f9209-8206-4ba2-bafd-9e6c3c325479}} mag, so we ascribe very little of the uncertainty in {{formula:91827a7a-0ce7-43c9-a1e8-e614344f28a6}} to this conversion.
The cause of the discrepancy: Arce & Goodman (1999) obtain the extinction toward the Taurus region using four different techniques. All four give similar results in terms of the absolute value and overall structure of the extinction. Most importantly, AG find that {{formula:183285b9-7c0e-4f19-bffd-addf65d77cbf}} agrees well with extinction values obtained by measuring the color excess of background stars for which spectral types are known, which is the the most direct and accurate way to measure reddening (see Figure 2 in AG). So, the question now is why does the SFD method give extinctions which differ from the four determinations of extinction made by AG?Absolute values. Although data reduction and zero point determination of the emission is very elaborate and accurate in the SFD method, the normalization of the reddening per unit flux density (conversion between {{formula:b2a0d003-1c2e-4f0c-8dd1-d6948d6f840f}} and {{formula:ccbffb5e-859f-4141-9080-ee76f39ee26b}} ) seems to overestimate the reddening in regions of high dust opacity. As explained above, SFD use the correlation between intrinsic color and the Mg{{formula:d7a905c2-96c8-4f64-b81d-9aab2490a76c}} line index in elliptical galaxies to convert from dust column density to reddening. It can be seen in Figure 6 of SFD that 90% of the 389 elliptical galaxies they use for the vs. Mg{{formula:78d34569-0ba0-42a2-9fb6-528f366677b2}} regression have {{formula:78f46cab-c3d9-47c4-93b6-d3a6e17b7dac}} values of less then 0.1 mag. Moreover it is clear from their Figure 6 that the fit is excellent for values of {{formula:d02ed076-b071-4211-bf3b-8ff1eee05b86}} less than 0.15 mag, but for {{formula:8ff990b1-4645-436a-bc4c-089af97780c2}} mag the fit starts to diverge for the few points that exist. Galaxies with {{formula:09568be2-6a2c-4359-b32a-10d701e1add6}} mag ({{formula:65288886-a201-4149-8a79-14bc2fc8ba67}} mag) seem to follow a trend leading to reddening values in regions with high dust opacity being overestimated. SFD state that the slight trend in the residual is not statistically significant, but that may be due to the fact that there are so few points with {{formula:6b3e728b-af63-418d-885a-85fd3c8ee0e6}} mag.Figure 6 in SFD shows only two points (galaxies) that have {{formula:54e64396-376a-40c4-a5f7-8e3d340efc3a}} mag. We use the point with {{formula:b9f6f6a6-3d7e-4b6f-86e8-52835c704527}} mag to asses the amount of overestimation by the SFD method in high reddening regions. Using Figure 6 in SFD and {{formula:b795f8b0-762d-4260-bc63-8e306995b2c9}} , with {{formula:57d402cf-6de9-4206-b76a-df2401fe9954}} , for an extinction of around 1 mag, the SFD method would overestimate the extinction, at 1.31 magnitudes. In fact, by comparing {{formula:7631354d-e08c-43e5-810e-6539bba80a35}} to {{formula:91843c27-b943-4f53-bc39-4f690d4f0a4f}} , we find the overestimation by SFD can be even more than that: when {{formula:296b924e-ca48-4fa9-a7c4-d5903029af8b}} is 1, {{formula:a1892f4a-a75a-44cc-9975-f5d058301edd}} is typically 1.5. Thus we are convinced that SFD overestimates the reddening value to lines of sights where the extinction is more than 0.5 mag. Such overestimation is due to the fact that in the sample of 389 galaxies most of them have {{formula:beaec544-10a4-4b38-af22-547d6af17152}} and very few have {{formula:c8529087-6da4-4ae7-9b6a-4a315ede31d4}} . This results in an accurate conversion between 100 emission and reddening for regions with very low extinction ({{formula:a9a2513f-aeb2-463b-b88c-721084992e24}} ), but a less accurate conversion where {{formula:0d249410-2213-4cd3-8627-769fe48d4ed6}} ({{formula:48e504af-4260-4504-84cc-415e117c173c}} mag).One could argue that the SFD method overestimates the extinction because we overestimate the value of {{formula:bbb4934d-ed42-4d69-b5ed-f20bd69bbff9}} , needed to convert {{formula:15a5fd79-0611-48e8-ac22-33b0f84e7066}} to {{formula:83026890-f4f2-4e49-9a72-fea92ec65ebe}} . We believe that is not so, since several independent studies indicate that the value of {{formula:25e934e0-9aa5-4909-bcd4-0742a5f5da54}} in the Taurus dark cloud complex is around 3.1 and that it stays constant through the region for lines of sight in which {{formula:66a003f7-999f-47e6-ae6f-6fd1fa48115d}} mag (Kenyon et al. 1994; Vrba & Rydgren 1985). Furthermore, {{formula:a877cb05-4571-41f5-abbe-aeab910789aa}} gives very good agreement between {{formula:f43123a6-986d-4066-919b-d1d6f31b87e1}} and extinction obtained using the color excess of background stars for which spectral types are known (AG).Structure. In Section 2, we noted that there are certain places where the traces of {{formula:b9a6cd92-cdda-4a2c-8dd8-983b7ca3a8fc}} and {{formula:9cb1bb1b-b0a2-4d6e-bf1a-4784673ded1b}} differ not only in value but also in structure.The most dramatic “structural" differences correspond to places where the cuts in Figure 1 intercept IRAS point sources. SFD remove point sources from the ISSA images before they use them, while AG do not. Both AG and SFD assume a single dust temperature for each line of sight. In AG's determination of {{formula:4b2da30b-6817-4eed-82da-538decda3824}} , the high 60 flux from IRAS point sources transforms into dust with high color temperature, which in turn causes an artificial dip in the extinction (see Wood et al. 1994 and references therein for more on this effect). We can see that SFD have done a good job at removing point sources by noticing that where {{formula:21fc996c-5865-4660-a9b5-bf541139a10a}} has artificial dips, {{formula:ef5c3acf-2dde-4579-91ed-15f588293983}} traces the real structure (also traced by the other methods in AG). Thus {{formula:5c7e5a88-2f50-4385-8e2e-2a69247099d8}} , unlike {{formula:eb1701cf-3c21-4c67-97ad-56ba27b509a2}} , is free of any unphysical extinction due to IRAS point sources.Less dramatic, but more curious, structural discrepancies between the two methods are seen near the extinction peaks in Figure 1. Although {{formula:76d461cd-1fdb-494d-8541-92e68da1c146}} is in general larger than {{formula:2147a02b-c0cb-466a-822a-46aa97466d5c}} by a factor of 1.3 to 1.5, it is important to realize that in some peaks {{formula:9b1dda59-8f00-405a-b3e7-82a94af42859}} is larger by a factor less than 1.3 and in others it is smaller than {{formula:e8ed82d9-28f6-48d7-a84e-86eb41350038}} . In addition the gaussian-looking extinction peaks traced by {{formula:afb05115-47be-44d7-a83d-12bb2d262b2e}} are wider than those traced by {{formula:ea12fb55-4609-4ffe-b55d-82d6ca47303d}} . Gaussian fits to the peaks associated with Tau M1 and L1506 for both traces in cut 1 show that both peaks traced by {{formula:cb546ea7-eaf6-4edd-83b3-6b1860b70fce}} have a FWHM wider than those of the peaks traced by {{formula:99b156c2-4d7e-476d-b521-5602877187ac}} by a factor of 1.3. This suggests that in regions of steep extinction gradients the reddening obtained from the SFD map has a lower resolution than the quoted 6.1.We believe that this “smearing" in the SFD maps is caused by the difference in resolution between the ISSA flux maps (6.1) and the COBE-limited color temperature maps (1.4) employed by SFD. In Figure 2 we plot the 100 emission ({{formula:9724b58d-536a-4175-a019-5b676823d357}} ) versus declination for a section of cut 1, where the rise in {{formula:4b24e86d-b752-4a96-aae1-cac44807fe60}} associated with Tau M1 and L1506 are clearly seen. The plot shows the traces of {{formula:ab9af88a-5ae3-49e0-8d35-9c0a12ee4c53}} obtained by SFD ({{formula:b38d31d4-6285-4dc9-b448-a3b43a48a722}} ) and by AG ({{formula:e7fe4944-c217-4073-bf4a-a34621c1ef93}} ) averaged over the {{formula:6a155298-faed-473d-8160-a99f9a9d657b}} 10 width (in R.A.) of the cut. It can clearly be seen that both traces are essentially equal, and that the peaks have the same width and height. Thus it is after both the dust color temperature and {{formula:b7cd61b2-b5f8-4798-908a-ea7cc6a25154}} have been used together to obtain the extinction, that the SFD method loses spatial resolution. Regions of steep extinction gradients are likely to have temperature gradients, but if the spatial resolution in the dust color temperature is {{formula:89160209-57f7-45b1-bc17-2e1e5e9e117d}} then it is unlikely that these gradients would be detected. If the temperature gradients are not accounted for when calculating reddening, the result is areas with lower effective resolution. Therefore, the fact that SFD use a dust color temperature map with a spatial resolution a factor of 14 larger than the {{formula:59f6c591-6c2b-464c-b441-e3079a4cf23e}} map results in a reddening map which does not have a constant spatial resolution of 6.1. Unfortunately the DIRBE instrument has a limiting resolution of {{formula:ef1fd66a-9ccc-401f-86bd-b57d60f2a7b6}} 1, so it is not possible to do better with data taken with that instrument.
Conclusion: We test the COBE/IRAS all-sky reddening map of Schlegel, Finkbeiner & Davis (1998) using the extinction study of Arce & Goodman (1999). In their study, AG use four different techniques to study the extinction in a region of the Taurus dark cloud complex. All four techniques give very similar results in terms of the value of {{formula:a95dfc55-7535-47f2-988d-83d65afa52b2}} and the structure in the extinction. Thus the results of AG can be considered a truthful representation of the extinction in this region, and can be used to test the reliability of the SFD reddening map.We compare the extinction obtained by AG using ISSA 60 and 100 images with the SFD reddening map. Our results show that in general the SFD method gives extinction values a factor of 1.3 to 1.5 larger than the extinction obtained by AG. We conclude that SFD overestimates the reddening value to lines of sights where {{formula:cd7d51a5-d158-4e84-b667-6700ccfadbb3}} mag. We expect this overestimation is caused by the fact that in the sample of 389 galaxies used to calculate a conversion from dust column density to {{formula:890541c3-f722-42ca-b447-f20e0c5e1bc0}} , 90% of the galaxies have low reddening values ({{formula:03c6c3c7-ef85-4960-9450-6fa6cc8fcf75}} ) and very few ({{formula:f60d39e3-f574-445f-b506-51e86badadbb}} %) have high reddening ({{formula:a5954bf4-f470-45ab-a465-33559d97a49d}} ) values. The lack of galaxies in high reddening regions results in inaccuracy in the conversion between dust column and reddening for lines of sight with {{formula:b1fb780c-c82f-4674-a3f5-ee5f48f7d62d}} . This bias should be studied in other regions of the sky in order to see how general this trend is. For now we advise that caution be taken when using the SFD all-sky reddening map to obtain reddening (and extinction) values for regions with {{formula:4c86555b-a5f9-4327-b009-5326822ba9e7}} ({{formula:32161b52-5dc6-47d6-b823-86f4dc2c9199}} mag), as the value given by SFD could be larger than the real value.The behavior of {{formula:695cb5d7-44aa-476d-a351-1a89ae21d5d2}} near steep gradients in extinction seems to be different from the overall “smoother” extinction regions. The difference between {{formula:b2bf80fd-ec3a-49f3-acba-fc8e16758107}} and {{formula:c5b04d9f-92b1-4ec5-b59b-382e690d8217}} decreases near extinction peaks and in some peaks {{formula:3ea980b1-b5e9-4c3e-887a-043d0b019136}} even becomes smaller than {{formula:384e4a74-67c2-4256-8eac-677a8c338235}} . In addition the peaks in {{formula:e0938dbe-cae8-4366-adbb-9189bf094ab6}} are wider than the {{formula:935ff682-cb04-471e-bb67-e6e2eb2b3acf}} peaks. We attribute this behavior to the fact that SFD use a dust temperature map with a spatial resolution of a factor of 14 larger than the 100 intensity map used to obtain the reddening map. The poor resolution in the temperature maps results in a reddening map which shows less spatial resolution near extinction peaks.We thank David Schlegel, Douglas Finkbeiner and Mark David for their very useful comments on this work, and Krzysztof Stanek for pointing out the SFD paper to us, and for sharing his work on this topic. claims.claim: Metal‑rich giant stars in the inner Galactic bulge show the largest deviations from theoretical isochrones toward higher temperatures when dereddened with the SFD map.
These deviations are caused by the SFD map over‑estimating the reddening in high‑extinction regions, so the dereddened colours become too blue and the inferred temperatures too high.

One limitation of the SFD map is that its empirical conversion from dust emission to reddening was calibrated using elliptical galaxies that mostly lie in low‑reddening environments, making the conversion inaccurate when A_V > ~0.5 mag.

Another limitation is the low spatial resolution of the dust‑temperature map (≈1.4°), which smooths small‑scale temperature structure and leads to systematic errors in regions of steep extinction gradients and high visual extinction.

paper1AloneSufficient.explanation: Paper 1 describes the construction flaws of the SFD map and how they cause reddening over‑estimates, but it does not discuss the observed temperature deviations of metal‑rich bulge giants or link the map errors to those specific stars.

paper2AloneSufficient.explanation: Paper 2 reports that the most metal‑rich bulge giants deviate from isochrones and mentions that the Schlegel reddening may be too high, but it does not provide the detailed technical reasons (calibration sample bias, temperature‑map resolution) for why the SFD map is inaccurate in high‑extinction regions.

paper1PlusQuestionSufficient.explanation: The question supplies the observational fact (metal‑rich giants deviate) but does not give the astrophysical context needed to interpret that fact; Paper 1 alone cannot explain why those particular stars are affected without the bulge‑star observations from Paper 2.

paper2PlusQuestionSufficient.explanation: The question states the phenomenon but does not contain the technical details of the SFD map’s construction; Paper 2 alone cannot answer which specific map limitations produce the artifact.

questionLeakage.explanation: The question states the observed deviation but does not provide the causal explanation or the map‑construction details; therefore no key fact needed for the answer is leaked.

redundancyOrArtifactOnly.explanation: Paper 2 mentions that the Schlegel map may be too high, but Paper 1 supplies the non‑redundant, detailed reasons (calibration bias and low temperature‑map resolution). Both contributions are necessary for a complete answer.

mainVsOptionalElaboration.explanation: Both papers are required for the central answer: Paper 2 provides the observational link between metal‑rich giants and the reddening correction, while Paper 1 provides the specific construction flaws that generate the over‑correction. Neither paper alone yields the full explanation.

multiHopValidity.explanation: Answering the question demands two distinct pieces of information that reside in separate papers. The ARGOS survey (Paper 2) documents that the most metal‑rich bulge giants deviate from isochrones after SFD‑based dereddening, establishing the phenomenon that must be explained. The test of the SFD map (Paper 1) supplies the precise technical shortcomings of the map—bias in the elliptical‑galaxy calibration and the coarse 1.4° dust‑temperature resolution—that cause systematic over‑estimation of reddening in high‑extinction regions, which in turn produces the observed temperature offsets. Neither paper alone can provide both the observational context and the map‑construction critique, and the question does not leak the answer. Consequently the question truly requires a multi‑hop combination of evidence, meeting the GOOD criterion.

thinking.step1Claim: The SFD all‑sky reddening map overestimates extinction in regions with A_V > 0.5 mag because its empirical conversion from dust emission to reddening is calibrated on a sample of elliptical galaxies that are almost all in low‑reddening environments, and because the dust colour‑temperature map used in the construction has a coarse spatial resolution (~1.4°) that smooths small‑scale temperature gradients, leading to systematic over‑estimation of reddening in high‑opacity areas.

step1NotTrivial.explanation: The claim is a detailed mechanism/limitation (calibration bias and resolution limitation), not merely the identification of a method or dataset, so it is non‑trivial.

step1LeakedByQuestion.explanation: The question asks for the specific limitations of the SFD map; it does not state them. Therefore the proposition must be derived from Paper A.

thinking.step2Claim: The most metal‑rich giant stars in the inner Galactic bulge show the largest offsets toward higher temperatures from theoretical isochrones when dereddened with the SFD map because the map’s over‑estimated reddening (especially in the highest‑extinction fields near the plane) makes the dereddened colours too blue, which drives the spectroscopic temperature scale upward and shifts the stars away from the isochrones.

strictDependency.explanation: To explain *why* the metal‑rich giants deviate, one must invoke the specific over‑estimation mechanism described in Step 1. Without knowing the calibration bias and resolution issue, the answer would be limited to “the map may be too high”, which does not fully answer the ‘why’ and the ‘what limitations’ part of the question.

entityLinking.explanation: The question is not merely linking the name of the SFD map to the observed deviation; it requires applying the mechanistic explanation from Paper A to interpret the observation in Paper B.

dependencyStrength.explanation: The question requires two consecutive reasoning steps. Step 1 extracts a non‑trivial mechanistic limitation of the SFD reddening map from Paper A (calibration bias and coarse temperature‑map resolution). Step 2 uses the observation from Paper B that metal‑rich bulge giants deviate from isochrones when dereddened with that map, and to answer the ‘why’ it must apply the specific limitation identified in Step 1. The question does not leak the Step 1 proposition, and the dependency is strict rather than mere entity linking. Therefore the multihop requirement is satisfied, yielding a GOOD judgement.

thinking.mainQuestion: Explain why the most metal‑rich giant stars in the inner Galactic bulge, when dereddened with the Schlegel, Finkbeiner & Davis (SFD) all‑sky reddening map, appear hotter than theoretical isochrones, and identify the specific construction limitations of the SFD map that produce this artifact in high‑extinction regions.

subquestions.question: What deviation do the most metal‑rich bulge giants show from theoretical isochrones after being dereddened with the SFD map?
What are the concrete limitations in the construction of the SFD reddening map that cause it to overestimate extinction in regions of high visual extinction?

concatenationOrComparison.explanation: The final answer is not a simple concatenation of two independent facts; it must connect the map’s limitations (over‑estimation of reddening due to calibration on low‑reddening ellipticals and low‑resolution dust‑temperature map) to the observed temperature offset of the metal‑rich giants.

onePartConstrainsOther.explanation: Understanding the specific SFD limitations directly explains why the dereddened colours of metal‑rich giants become too blue, leading to higher inferred temperatures. Thus the answer to the second sub‑question constrains and enables the explanation required for the first.

artificialIntegration.explanation: The question is not merely appearing integrated because it mentions two papers; genuine reasoning must combine the observational result (Paper 2) with the methodological flaws of the SFD map (Paper 1) to answer the ‘why’.

necessaryExplanatoryBridge.explanation: A true explanatory bridge is needed: the over‑estimated reddening from the SFD map (due to its calibration sample and coarse temperature resolution) leads to over‑correction of stellar colours, making the stars appear hotter than the isochrones predict.

nonDecomposability.explanation: The question requires multi‑step synthesis. While each component can be answered from a single paper, the overall answer must link the map’s construction flaws to the observed temperature offset of metal‑rich bulge giants. Solving the second part (map limitations) is essential to explain the first part (deviation), meaning the sub‑questions are not independent. Therefore the question is non‑decomposable and fulfills the GOOD criterion.

evidenceNeeded: Empirical observation that the most metal‑rich giant stars in the inner Galactic bulge, when dereddened with the SFD all‑sky reddening map, lie far to the blue (higher temperature) side of theoretical isochrones.
Quantitative statement that this effect is strongest for stars in regions of high visual extinction (A_V > ~0.5 mag).

Explanation that the SFD map overestimates reddening in such high‑extinction regions because its empirical conversion from far‑infrared dust emission to E(B‑V) was calibrated on elliptical galaxies that mostly inhabit low‑reddening sightlines.

Explanation that the SFD dust‑temperature component of the map has a coarse spatial resolution (~1.4°), which smooths temperature gradients and further degrades the accuracy of the reddening estimate in areas with steep extinction gradients.
Logical chain linking the over‑estimated reddening to an overly large dereddening correction, producing colours that are too blue and therefore inferred stellar temperatures that are too high.
evidencePaper1: Shows that the SFD map overestimates reddening by a factor of 1.3–1.5 in regions where A_V > 0.5 mag (the same regime where the bulge giants show the largest isochrone offsets).

Identifies two specific construction limitations of the SFD map: (a) the calibration of the dust‑to‑reddening conversion uses 389 elliptical galaxies, 90 % of which have E(B‑V) < 0.1 mag, making the relation unreliable at higher reddening; (b) the dust colour‑temperature map used in the conversion has a spatial resolution of 1.4°, causing loss of small‑scale temperature structure and under‑resolution of steep extinction gradients.
Explains that these limitations lead to systematic over‑estimation of reddening in high‑extinction sightlines, which directly produces the artefact described in the question.
evidencePaper2: Provides the observational result that metal‑rich ([Fe/H] ≳ 0) red‑clump giants in the inner bulge deviate progressively more from BaSTI isochrones as metallicity increases, with the largest temperature offsets seen for the most metal‑rich stars.

Notes that the most metal‑rich stars are found in fields with the highest Schlegel reddening values, and discusses the possibility that an over‑estimated SFD reddening could be responsible for the observed isochrone offsets.
Thus supplies the phenomenon that needs to be explained by the limitations identified in Paper 1.

paperDominance.explanation: Paper 2 supplies the empirical observation of the temperature deviation for metal‑rich bulge giants, while Paper 1 supplies the mechanistic explanation of why the SFD map is inaccurate in high‑extinction regions. Neither paper alone can answer the full question.

informationRedundancy.explanation: The two papers contribute distinct pieces of information: Paper 2 describes the stellar‑population phenomenon, and Paper 1 details the specific construction flaws of the SFD map that cause the artefact. There is no overlap in the content they provide.

artifactOnlyEvidence.explanation: Both papers provide substantive, non‑trivial evidence. answerClaims.claim: This systematic offset is caused by the SFD map overestimating interstellar extinction in high‑opacity regions.
answerClaims.evidence: The SFD test paper reports that the map overestimates reddening by a factor of 1.3–1.5 for A_V > 0.5 mag, and the ARGOS paper mentions that “some authors argue that the Schlegel reddening may be too high” in such regions.

answerClaims.claim: The map’s empirical conversion from dust emission to reddening was calibrated using elliptical galaxies that almost all lie in low‑reddening environments, so the relation becomes inaccurate where visual extinction exceeds about half a magnitude.
answerClaims.evidence: The SFD paper describes the conversion using the Mg line strength of 389 elliptical galaxies, 90 % of which have E(B‑V) < 0.1 mag, leading to inaccuracy at higher reddening (A_V > 0.5 mag).

answerClaims.claim: The temperature map used in the SFD construction has a spatial resolution of only about 1.4°; this coarse resolution blurs small‑scale temperature structure and worsens errors in high‑extinction areas.
answerClaims.evidence: The SFD description states that the dust colour‑temperature map has a resolution of 1.4°, and that this low resolution causes “smearing” and loss of detail in regions with steep extinction gradients.

First 15000 characters: Local Analysis of Inverse Problems: H\"{o}lder Stability and Iterative Reconstruction
abstract: We consider a class of inverse problems defined by a nonlinear map from parameter or model functions to the data. We assume that solutions exist. The space of model functions is a Banach space which is smooth and uniformly convex; however, the data space can be an arbitrary Banach space. We study sequences of parameter functions generated by a nonlinear Landweber iteration and conditions under which these strongly converge, locally, to the solutions within an appropriate distance. We express the conditions for convergence in terms of H\"{o}lder stability of the inverse maps, which ties naturally to the analysis of inverse problems.
Introduction: In this paper, we study the convergence of certain nonlinear iterative reconstruction methods for inverse problems in Banach spaces. We consider a class of inverse problems defined by a nonlinear map from parameter or model functions to the data. The parameter functions and data are contained in certain Banach spaces, or Hilbert spaces, respectively. We explicitly construct sequences of parameter functions by a Landweber iteration. Our analysis pertains to obtaining natural conditions for the strong convergence of these sequences (locally) to the solutions in an appropriate distance measure.Our main result establishes convergence of the Landweber iteration if the inverse problem ensures a Hölder stability estimate. Moreover, we prove monotonicity of the residuals defined by the sequence induced by the iteration. We also obtain the convergence rates without so-called source and nonlinearity conditions. The stability condition is a natural one in the framework of iterative reconstruction.Extensive research has been carried out to study convergence of the Landweber iteration and its modifications. In the case of model and data spaces being Hilbert, see Hanke, Neubauer & Scherzer . An overview of iterative methods for inverse problems in Hilbert spaces can be found, for example, in Kaltenbacher, Neubauer & Scherzer . Schöpfer, Louis & Schuster presented a nonlinear extension of the Landweber method to Banach spaces using duality mappings. We use this iterative method in the analysis presented here. Duality mappings also play a role in iterative schemes for monotone and accretive operators (see Alber , Chidume & Zegeye and Zeidler , ). The model space needs to be smooth and uniformly convex, however, the data space can be an arbitrary Banach space. Due to the geometrical characteristics of Banach spaces other than Hilbert spaces, it is more appropriate to use Bregman distances rather than Ljapunov functionals to prove convergence (Osher et al. ). For convergence rates, see Hofmann et al. . Schöpfer, Louis & Schuster furthermore considered the solution of convex split feasibility problems in Banach spaces by cyclic projections. Under the so-called tangential cone condition, pertaining to the nonlinear map modelling the data, convergence has been established; invoking a source condition in a convergence rate result. Here, we build on the work of Kaltenbacher, Schöpfer and Schuster and revisit these conditions with a view to stability properties of the inverse problem.In many inverse problems one probes a medium, or an obstacle, with a particular type of field and measures the response. From these measurements one aims to determine the medium properties and/or (geometrical) structure. Typically, the physical phenomenon is modeled by partial differential equations and the medium properties by variable, and possibly singular, coefficients. The interaction of fields is usually restricted to a bounded domain with boundary. Experiments can be carried out on the boundary. The goal is thus to infer information on the coefficients in the interior of the domain from the associated boundary measurements. The map, solving the partial differential equations, from coefficients or parameter functions to the measurements or data is nonlinear. Its injectivity is studied in the analysis of inverse problems. As an example, we discuss Electrical Impedance Tomography, where the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map represents the data, and summarize the conditions leading to Lipschitz stability.Traditionally, the Landweber iteration has been viewed as a fixed-point iteration. However, in general, for inverse problems, the underlying fixed point operator is not a contraction. There is an extensive literature of iterative methods for approximating fixed points of non-expansive operators. Hanke, Neubauer & Scherzer replace the condition of non-expansive to a local tangential cone condition, which guarantees a local result. In the finite-dimensional setting, in which, for example the model space is {{formula:5839680f-660f-4976-84e0-438d41d3065c}} , non-convex constraint optimization problems admitting iterative solutions have been studied by Curtis et al. . Under certain assumptions, they obtain convergence to stationary points of the associated feasibility problem. In the context of inverse problems defined by partial differential equations, this setting is motivated by discretizing the problems prior to studying the convergence (locally) of the iterations. Inequality constraints are necessary to enforce locality. The non-convexity is addressed by Hessian modifications based on inertia tests.The paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we summarize certain geometrical aspects of Banach spaces, including (uniform) smoothness and (uniform) convexity, and their connection to duality mappings. Smoothness is naturally related to Gâteaux differentiability. We also introduce the Bregman distance. We then define the nonlinear Landweber iteration in Banach spaces. In Section we introduce the basic assumptions including Hölder stability and analyze the convergence of the Landweber iteration in Hilbert spaces. In Section we adapt these assumptions and generalize the analysis of convergence of the Landweber iteration to Banach spaces. We also establish the convergence rates. In Section we give an example, namely, the reconstruction of conductivity in Electrical Impedance Tomography, and show that our assumptions can be satisfied.

First 15000 characters: Stable reconstruction of the volatility in a regime-switching local volatility model
abstract: Prices of European call options in a regime-switching local volatility model can be computed by solving a parabolic system which generalises the classical Black and Scholes equation, giving these prices as functionals of the local volatilities. We prove Lipschitz stability for the inverse problem of determining the local volatilities from quoted call option prices for a range of strikes, if the calls are indexed by the different states of the continuous Markov chain which governs the regime switches.
Introduction and main result: As is known since the fundamental work of Black, Scholes and Merton, prices of European options and other financial derivatives can be computed by solving a final value problem for a parabolic linear partial differential equation (PDE) known as the Black and Scholes equation. The coefficients of this PDE will depend on the stochastic model, in the form of a stochastic differential equation or SDE driven by one or more Brownian motions, for the underlying asset of the derivative. Conversely, for derivative contracts which are liquidly traded, one would like to use the market-quoted derivative prices to infer information about the (parameters of the) underlying stochastic model. Once the latter are known, the model can be used to price less liquidly traded derivatives, including derivatives which are not market-quoted but privately exchanged between two parties (the so-called `Over-the-Counter' contracts). Inferring the model from observed prices is known as the calibration problem. By what we have just said, it is clear that the calibration problem for derivatives can be interpreted as an inverse PDE problem, that of determining one or more coefficients of a parabolic PDE from the observation of certain of its solutions. Consequently, the various techniques that have been developed to study inverse PDE problems can be made to bear on calibration. This point of view was first elaborated by Bouchouev and Isakov , , who examined the problem of reconstructing the, by assumption time-independent, local volatility function of a so-called Local Volatility model from European call option prices of a fixed maturity but arbitrary strike, these prices being observed at some given point in time (and hence for some given value of the price of the underlying asset). We recall that a Local Volatility (LV) model for the price of a risky asset is Brownian motion-driven SDE in which the diffusion coefficient is itself a function of the asset-price and possibly also of time. Bouchouev and Isakov established unicity and, under additional assumptions, stability in Hölder norms. An essential ingredient in their work was Dupire's PDE for European calls as functions of their strikes and maturities.In this paper we will prove a Sobolev-norm version of Bouchouev's and Isakov's stability estimate. Moreover, we will do so for a larger class of models called Regime Switching Local Volatility or RSLV models, also known as Markov Modulated Local Volatility models. These generalise the Local Volatility models by allowing the local volatility function to jump according to an independent continuous-time Markov chain, thereby incorporating features of a Stochastic Volatility or SV model.The stochastic ingredients of a RSLV model are a Brownian motion {{formula:bcccba47-ca2f-437f-bd99-d7d62c9bb814}} and an independent finite state continuous time Markov process {{formula:92fcd8a8-8b8f-42cc-b2f2-90c89c3111b3}} with state spaceSome authors, following , realise the states {{formula:274f7c5c-3304-40d1-8926-2cf616bebead}} as the canonical basis vectors of {{formula:9e6eebef-60aa-4947-93e0-632cafa2a9df}} (which amounts to identifying {{formula:8e63f196-b5df-437e-ac91-9bae68c19ca8}} with the function {{formula:7a0fd051-c6fa-4734-9476-fd7f7ceacdae}} introduced below). Such a model can be regarded as a simple type of stochastic volatility model, in which the stochastic driver of the volatility is a Markov chain instead of the Brownian motion which is traditionally used for stochastic volatility models, such as the models of Hull and White, of Stein and Stein and of Heston or the SABR model. Option pricing in regime-switching diffusion models is attracting an increasing interest in the literature: we mention as an early reference, and as more recent ones , , , , , , , .One possible, and popular, economic interpretation of the model is that the state space {{formula:d1d3f936-5739-4439-b8fe-4a7fefd5b0bd}} of the Markov chain represents different global states of the economy, for example, different phases of a business cycle. In each of these phases, which correspond to the different states {{formula:662a8e3d-f4d9-4226-bf7d-de369fb6387c}} of the Markov chain, the price {{formula:70289894-a4c3-4322-8f67-d86357fded74}} of the underlying asset evolves according to a Local Volatility model with volatility function {{formula:1872f6c8-005e-4881-b01a-21830f78681b}} and interest rate and dividend rates {{formula:cfb4988c-8c80-40db-9507-daaafeaf53d2}} , {{formula:b6bdb1f8-4425-4a80-bca7-cc8a9983b1c4}} For example, the risk-free base rate, as set by a Central Bank, tends to be low during a recession, and high during an economic boom, and one would expect the opposite behaviour for the dividend rate. In case {{formula:6e7e6217-c0f4-4428-80df-3db597cd2b76}} is injective, investors can effectively observe the different states of the Markov chain. If not, we are dealing with a Hidden Markov model. In this paper we will assume that the Markov chain is observable. We will moreover assume that there exist European call options with a state dependent pay-off which again allows one to distinguish the different states.
