Also less massive galaxies are affected more strongly by tidal forces. For group environments, there is evidence that the tidal forces also influence the ram pressure stripping efficiency (, ). We have, however, chosen a massive galaxy (rotation velocity {{formula:d60f6f8c-3c2d-4890-8adc-2cb377cabe52}} ) and follow only the first orbit in a cluster environment. Thus we expect that tidal forces play a secondary role in our case, although there may be some influence. Similar to paper I, presented SPH simulations of RPS of a galaxy orbiting through cluster. They modelled the ICM-ISM interaction only near the cluster centre, but included the mutual gravity of all gaseous and non-gaseous galactic particles as well as the gravitation of the cluster potential. They did not find a significant influence on the stellar and DM components. Thus, we expect that our treatment yields reasonable results.The orbit of the galaxy is determined by integrating the motion of a point mass through the gravitational potential of the cluster. In the course of the simulation, the position of the galaxy potential is shifted along this orbit.
Code: The simulations were performed with the FLASH code () version 2.5, a multidimensional adaptive mesh refinement hydrodynamics code. It solves the Riemann problem on a Cartesian grid using the Piecewise-Parabolic Method (PPM). The simulations presented here are performed in 3D. The gas obeys the ideal equation of state with an adiabatic index of {{formula:af7242c6-7fc8-44ae-b565-88865eccf24c}} . The size of the simulation box is chosen such that the galaxy's orbit during the simulation time (3 Gyr) fits into the grid. Depending on the orbit, the size of the simulation box ranges between {{formula:1397f20d-9769-482a-b356-e7455c5c3fa0}} and {{formula:6009570e-f7d0-44d9-9d48-c446f692d351}} . All boundaries are reflecting.The coarsest refinement level has a resolution of {{formula:0791e625-4df0-4327-892c-109df6a4f168}} . For most runs, we use 8 levels of refinement, i.e. the best resolution is {{formula:a4db06ab-1dc9-43f1-b99c-c4ee1c995e60}} . In addition to the standard density and pressure gradient criteria, our user-defined refinement criteria enforce maximal refinement on the galactic gas disc and enforce stepwise de-refinement with increasing distance to the galaxy. Details are described in paper I. The important point for the investigation of the wakes is that we limit the refinement outside {{formula:1295c4e5-d0a7-428e-b409-8e004abd03d7}} around galaxy centre to {{formula:50d0a767-1a09-4507-b70b-aa0a5bacd339}} (6 refinement levels), and we limit the refinement outside {{formula:453fe2dc-c9dd-40d7-9f80-390256bdab6b}} around galaxy centre to {{formula:d5fa2d1d-af8c-4564-b8d6-b465c1a9958a}} (3 refinement levels). Together with the standard refinement criteria, this leads to a typical resolution of {{formula:b7e37ea6-bf64-42ab-bafe-018f5bcdf693}} at {{formula:b8395ae9-1ad1-48a5-a073-bf0d100f7002}} behind the galaxy. Given our resolution restriction, our analysis and discussion of the wake properties is restricted to the first {{formula:76fea7d0-d346-4560-87c7-7be4300e9212}} behind the galaxy. A discussion of the influence of the resolution on our results is given in App. , we find our results not to be sensitive to resolution.The FLASH code offers the opportunity to advect mass scalars along with the density. In order to be able to identify the galactic gas after it is stripped from the galaxy, we utilise a mass scalar, {{formula:08fe7c3a-7e2d-4cf2-90e7-68c35fa60881}} , to contain the fraction of galactic gas in each cell. Initially, this array has the value 1 in the region of the galactic disc and 0 elsewhere. As a result, every cell where {{formula:b8b50b33-07af-4f78-a9c2-9f5cfaacc9e5}} contains a certain amount of gas that has originally been inside the galaxy. At each time-step, the quantity {{formula:b27f1660-ce01-4281-bc2f-c37a6f24569f}} gives the local density of galactic gas. In the context of this paper, we will refer to this gas as galactic gas or ISM even if it has left the galaxy.
Model galaxy: The galaxy model is the same as in and paper I, i.e. a massive spiral with a flat rotation curve at {{formula:6f216407-1f9e-4ec6-be0f-762f2aa7d140}} . It consists of a dark matter halo ({{formula:9cc9b707-5092-4724-aa91-47221435f35a}} within {{formula:4404eb5c-02e4-46fe-b263-87f91a8b8d3f}} ), a stellar bulge ({{formula:a88d301a-d5c5-4d86-98d7-68c1486f9bec}} ), a stellar disc ({{formula:81dbe040-b5ba-4d4c-8625-9112362d3c88}} ) and a gaseous disc ({{formula:9fff2340-e5ea-4c68-8d2b-3e982e259515}} ). All non-gaseous components just provide the galaxy's potential and are not evolved during the simulation. For a description of the individual components and a list of parameters please refer to RB06.
Cluster model: The cluster is set in hydrostatic equilibrium, where the density of the ICM follows a {{formula:921c0fd8-cd33-4b1d-8b8f-6d7dc2401328}} -profile, {{formula:1b76b774-7180-422d-b591-f15f164f4da2}}while the ICM temperature is constant. Given the density and temperature distribution and thus pressure distribution throughout the cluster, the underlying gravitational acceleration due to the cluster potential is calculated from the hydrostatic equation. Here we present simulations for three clusters. The parameters are listed in Table REF along with two parameter sets for the Virgo cluster from the literature. {{table:7661a461-25da-4e91-9685-fde3032bb89e}}{{figure:0e180a93-70cf-48d8-a266-73f1012fd5ce}}Figure REF shows the density and pressure profiles of clusters C1 and C3. The only difference between clusters C1 and C2 is a factor of 2 in density. These two clusters are compact, the ICM density is strongly peaked. Thus, they are similar to the Virgo cluster, but not as extreme as Virgo (see Fig. REF ). Cluster C3 resembles the Coma cluster (parameters see ), which is very extended.
Galaxy orbit: The orbit of the galaxy determines its ram pressure history. We aimed at constructing orbits with medium to high ram pressure peaks, i.e. where the galaxy is expected to lose a significant fraction of its gas or is even stripped completely. We concentrate on orbits of galaxies that could be regarded as falling into the cluster for the first time, i.e. they start from a sufficiently large distance from the cluster centre. Additionally, the galaxies are bound to the cluster.Here we present simulations for four orbits that are summarised in Fig. REF . {{figure:b3ba9d14-c169-4060-8bc2-38bd36fe4c2a}}Three of these orbits are highly radial, whereas the fourth has a large impact parameter. The labels of the runs represent the cluster (C+number), small or large impact parameter (SM or LG), fast or slow galaxy (FST or SLW), inclination (F for near face-on, M for medium, E for near edge-on; FE for first near face-on but then near edge-on, etc.). In all cases, the galaxy orbits in the {{formula:   Last 15615 characters: }} in the Virgo cluster rest frame, which is rather high. However, assuming a much smaller component in the plane of the sky would increase the true length of the HI tail a lot. Our current assumption already results in a true length of the HI tail of {{formula:bd45cef5-fd59-4685-b68e-dc1641065a1f}} .A reasonable value for the local ICM density at the position of NGC 4388 is a few {{formula:93e372ab-f9cb-4761-99b5-4b0c484923c0}} . With a likely velocity of about {{formula:7ec3845d-f066-4e98-925b-d563b943c274}} , it experiences a ram pressure of about {{formula:7426cc5f-9758-470d-a678-4df76d496e51}} . According to our simulations, this is enough to be stripped heavily, so regarding the degree of stripping, simulations and observations agree.Regarding the combination of orbital velocity and local ICM density, in our simulations, there is no case directly comparable to NGC 4388. The closest our simulations get to the velocity-density combination of NGC 4388 is the peri-centre passage of runs C1-LG-FST-...or at {{formula:789c47f5-2da0-4333-857b-0eacc44ed080}} of run C3-SM-FST-MF. In both cases, the ram pressure is about {{formula:2478c4b5-03ff-4e10-8cc5-ecddb4a2fae7}} , but the orbital velocity is only slightly below {{formula:6b22122e-e7fa-4550-a7b3-e489a2454353}} . In both cases, the mass loss per orbital length is about {{formula:fcbbd67e-d08f-4b93-be79-330b0370c89d}} . Given that NGC 4388 is probably a factor of {{formula:516dd457-a902-4c60-bc16-cac3009e93ff}} faster than the two mentioned examples, also the mass loss per orbital length should be a factor of {{formula:b4d665b5-69c5-4b13-91ef-b74aa3d03a77}} smaller, which would lead to a less dense tail than the ones in the mentioned runs. As an opposing effect, the line-of-sight and the tail of NGC 4388 make an angle of about 45o, so that projected densities appear a factor of {{formula:cf976b36-bd8b-4539-92b0-4e093f464452}} higher than they would if the line-of-sight and the tail were perpendicular to each other. Also the projected gas mass per orbital length is about {{formula:4aa84bd4-8e40-4e53-a163-8e1b2977dd13}} times higher. As these two effects cancel each other, we expect column densities and gas masses per orbital length comparable to the ones in our simulations. Thus, our simulations predict that the column density in the tail near the galaxy should be near {{formula:d2bc5d62-8b8f-4e27-a3b7-13051a3737bc}} , and decrease gradually with increasing distance to the galaxy to below {{formula:7b0b3788-b2e1-4993-a55e-5c9bfbedc614}} at a distance of {{formula:5920dc14-6988-4c13-a1ed-b6e9390730f3}} or latest {{formula:1d1be106-021f-49e5-8eb5-9db2f6aba6a7}} behind the galaxy. At a distance of {{formula:9eab1e06-9eef-468e-ac56-245b9e476620}} , the gas mass per orbital length should correspond to the galaxy's mass loss per orbital length, which we estimated above to be about {{formula:c6a8b7f6-cae5-4726-90b8-94804011eb50}} .However, the tail of NGC 4388 looks different. It is densest at a distance of {{formula:91e769ee-7b95-4d93-85fc-38015165bbe7}} behind the galaxy, here the column density reaches {{formula:056504db-e49c-4f53-b2ea-f9925c2ef96f}} . The spatial width of this dense patch is about {{formula:5cc74cc4-2e70-4d16-9a9b-c0ef4b807439}} , thus this dense patch corresponds to a mass per orbital length of about {{formula:bd0403c7-9108-40d9-bfe7-54737e09ee67}} . Towards the galaxy, the column density as well as the mass per orbital length decrease. In HI, the tail even shows a gap near the galaxy. In this gap, observed a plume of ionised gas. However, the total mass of this plume is only {{formula:0302f404-2a43-43ec-a18a-70c599c37cda}} , which corresponds to a mass per orbital length to {{formula:dac2e980-999a-4a7f-a0f9-c68f9f14a741}} and is much less than we expected. Thus, the distribution of stripped gas along the tail differs from what we expect.The width of the tail shows some flaring. In our simulations, we do not observe tail flaring in the sensitivity limit of these simulations. In the simulations, the tails show flaring only at much lower column densities.The ionised part of the tail NGC 4388 shows a filamentary structure. On the basis of a deep spectroscopic study, derive the H{{formula:695a2f8d-3d5c-4962-953f-ec453eca15fe}} velocity field, which turns out to be quite complicated. The authors identify several kinematic groups among the filaments. However, they also consider significant turbulent motions possible. They argue that the kinematic structure and metallicity of the ionisation are not well-explained by a minor-merger scenario, but can be explained naturally by ram pressure stripping and an additional starburst driven superwind in the galactic nucleus. According to our simulations, turbulent motions in the tail are very likely. However, the mass of stripped gas near the galaxy is much less than we expected.The HI tail of NGC 4388 () remains hard to fit with the simulations also with respect to the velocity information. The velocity width of the tail is rather small over the whole length. Additionally, according to our simulations, the acceleration of the stripped gas towards the ICM velocity is finished approximately at a distance of {{formula:264c95c7-bc97-4fa7-bc7c-3aabaf327ef7}} behind the galaxy. For NGC 4388, however, the velocity of at the end of the tail differs from the galaxy's systemic velocity only by {{formula:e5ab195d-45d8-42fe-9ffd-ce0a2e56e227}} . According to our simulations, a value comparable to the galaxy's radial velocity with respect to the cluster mean, {{formula:ff210091-2f32-4c17-81df-b806932a75c5}} , would be expected.In summary, our simulations have difficulties to explain the details of NGC 4388's tail, where the most severe points are:The distribution of stripped gas along the tail differs between observations and simulations. The simulations predict much more gas near the galaxy. The mass per orbital length at a distance of {{formula:6a612708-0b79-4db4-b15d-8a7227395bc7}} behind the galaxy is approximately at the expected level, however, here the gas is confined in a smaller volume than expected and thus shows higher column densities than expected. According to our simulations, the stripped gas should be decelerated to the cluster mean velocity at a distance of {{formula:27bf9722-e585-401a-8bd9-8ae08d2f1ebf}} . According to the HI data, for NGC 4388, however, the stripped gas seems to have lost only 1/3 of the expected velocity change. In contrast to this, the H{{formula:993213ea-018e-45cf-a5c8-3c8b54cff380}} tail shows a velocity gradient as expected from our simulations. Radial velocities at the end of the H{{formula:83d89949-96b5-48b2-abce-cc70719299d9}} tail have already reached 300 to {{formula:8c3e8f58-4aa2-4471-9241-0f93532dc459}} . Also the turbulent structure of the H{{formula:9d010295-26f1-4817-87c0-fffe2b1985d5}} velocity field is in agreement with our simulations. We note that here the HI and the H{{formula:94a539be-30f5-4841-bac5-5ad7aebd7f66}} data seem to be in disagreement.There are several reasons that could cause the mismatches between the simulations and the observations. E.g. the ICM may not be smooth but inhomogeneous, and there may be ambient motions in the ICM, thus leading to a special ram pressure history of this galaxy. The Virgo spiral NGC 4522 is another example that suggests ambient motions in the ICM, as its degree of stripping implies a much stronger ram pressure than expected at its position in the cluster (). Moreover, NGC 4388 has an active nucleus and a starburst driven superwind (see and references therein), which will influence the dynamics of the ICM-ISM interaction. Additionally, our simulations cannot predict the temperature of the stripped gas and are thus unable to predict in which wavelengths the stripped gas is observable. However, the close vicinity of the galaxy has been searched for ionised and neutral gas and the amounts found are significantly less than what we expect.
H{{formula:133f4dbf-5f91-4f56-9b02-8be713a07827}}  and X-ray tails: Up to date, only a few galaxies with H{{formula:bda68363-9bb2-495d-bdaa-46f0255666ad}} and X-ray tails are known. There are two irregular galaxies in the cluster A 1367 that have H{{formula:12cdbd51-1877-4152-ab37-8d508cac5bbb}} tails of {{formula:8c3ecfd4-4820-45db-8979-4932bc5d4bad}} and {{formula:c69f4d29-8bee-4f4d-9242-8834ae86da2e}} length and {{formula:60e7c272-3ba0-433b-8b2b-08693e0a0316}} width (). The tails are straight and show some filamentary structure along the tail. have observed the Coma galaxy D 100 and found an H{{formula:59bc1457-ee2d-4e4d-aee1-1d500002b8c9}} tail that is exceptionally straight and narrow ({{formula:04e3b3f9-64e9-4044-9ae5-35923de471b9}} long, {{formula:e7aadc93-e64c-49ab-926f-528784f5c2e3}} wide). The H{{formula:a587f0db-d075-412f-97cc-577643db65f5}} tail of NGC 4388 has been discussed above in connection with its HI tail.have presented a long and narrow X-ray tail ({{formula:e1b5fe89-7380-4f47-ac3a-52eca1c2802f}} long, {{formula:988cd812-97f7-43dc-a5bf-ed0642e4a790}} wide) for the galaxy ESO 137-001 in the Coma-like cluster A 3627. Additionally, have found a {{formula:cafc7d2a-19aa-496d-933c-f369b1364b5f}} H{{formula:33ba1b20-f4fb-4aa7-9abf-641726126106}} tail for the same galaxy that coincides spatially with the X-ray tail. The mass of the X-ray tail is estimated to be {{formula:f44b5187-cf65-410b-aa9c-765579cc9d83}} , the H{{formula:070795fc-18b5-4735-b3e9-33ec7a09d260}} tail provides another few {{formula:ffcf7e1b-49ad-426c-8861-cbb0341c12de}} . Both, the X-ray and the H{{formula:bd60807c-0ccb-4563-a341-de5afe38ef77}} tail are nearly straight, although some very slight oscillation can be detected. In both wavebands, the highest emission is found near the galaxy, but there are some more brighter patches further downstream. If the brightness also traces the local gas mass, this behaviour would be expected if these tails are caused by ram pressure stripping. Also the total gas mass of the tails matches the ram pressure picture.A characteristic feature of the observed H{{formula:65942677-04e4-4781-8398-6e2909e3333d}} and X-ray tails is their narrowness and straightness. Given that our simulations cannot estimate the temperature of the stripped gas, we are unable to predict the brightness distribution of our tails in H{{formula:b8ea4160-30ba-40c1-a3bd-dd76d0f1719f}} or in X-rays. However, the projected density maps presented in this paper generally show much broader tails and make such narrow and straight tails difficult to understand. Although our simulations provide an important step towards a realistic description of RPS by modelling the flight through a cluster, still important physics seems to be missing.
Summary: We have performed 3D hydrodynamical simulations of ram pressure stripping of disc galaxies on orbits through galaxy clusters. Here we have presented a detailed study of the wakes associated with these galaxies.For a sensitivity limit typical for current HI observations ({{formula:4da4f7e0-94cd-43d9-9af0-02af16b0ca60}} ), we find that a typical tail length in projected gas density is {{formula:11f678fb-8998-4ecd-bb07-d8410254d47c}} . In this sensitivity limit, the width of the tails is similar to the galaxy's width with respect to the tail direction. Our simulations show that the density and length of the tail is not determined by the current ram pressure and thus temporal mass loss rate alone, but also by the galaxy's velocity. These two dependencies can be summarised in the mass loss per orbital length, which is the crucial parameter that determines the tail length and density.If we consider projected gas densities below the sensitivity limit, the tails show a flaring width, where the flaring ratio depends on the galaxy's cross-section with respect to its direction of motion. Large cross-sections lead to strong flaring, while for small cross-sections the flaring is weak. The flaring is caused by turbulence in the galactic wakes.The velocity in our wakes shows a significant turbulent component of a few {{formula:bd3c4522-169c-4e41-8275-6ae5113b73b7}} . The stripped gas is fully decelerated to the ICM rest frame at a distance of {{formula:894ffbaf-d529-4ba4-ba07-425d7caa488a}} behind the galaxy.We find that the stripped gas does not follow the galaxy for a long way but remains within {{formula:edf1344c-6b2e-4cba-8d3f-354c0da1d7c8}} from the position where it is lost. We have investigated in how far the deceleration of the galaxy by the drag force can be a heating source for the ICM and found that no significant effect is expected.As our simulations neglect thermal conduction, cooling and viscosity, they are unable to predict the wavelength at which the galactic wakes should be observable. Nonetheless, we compared our simulations with observations of galactic wakes.We can reproduce tails of {{formula:7fd93892-770b-4078-b174-21b73a1951b4}} length at cluster-centric distances between {{formula:c1d3648b-9321-4b2a-8165-a5fb7bfd28eb}} and {{formula:c34d2293-7100-4580-a296-abfa49509543}} in a compact cluster similar to the Virgo cluster. Thus we conclude that the galactic tails found by could indeed be formed by ram pressure stripping. However, our simulations have difficulties in reproducing the velocity information of these galaxies. The observations suggest that RPS proceeds less turbulent than in our simulations. Also, the structure of the wake of the Virgo spiral NGC 4388 is hard to explain by our simulations, not only due to shortcomings of our simulations, but also due to intrinsic discrepancies in this galaxy's data. This HI “tail” may not be caused by RPS at all, or this galaxy may have experienced a complex ram pressure history. Given that our simulations cannot predict the correct gas temperatures, comparisons to the H{{formula:bc61ba9f-2abe-42f6-b6f7-c860dee3ee08}} and X-ray tails are especially difficult. However, our simulations do not seem to be able to match the straightness and narrowness of these tails. Also these observations suggest that some physics that were neglected in our model, e.g. viscosity, cooling, and tidal interactions, may play an important role for the detailed structure of ram pressure stripping tails.

claims.claim: The 6 cm polarized radio continuum ridge, flat spectral index, and east‑to‑west polarization gradient indicate a large‑scale shock caused by active ram‑pressure compression in NGC 4522.

At the large projected cluster‑centric distance of NGC 4522, the smooth ICM density would be insufficient to produce the observed stripping; therefore the local ICM must be denser or have a higher relative velocity because of inhomogeneities or ambient motions.

Together, the observations imply that NGC 4522 is currently undergoing strong, active ram‑pressure stripping and that this interaction is made possible by an enhanced, locally disturbed ICM rather than the average smooth ICM.

paper1AloneSufficient.explanation: Paper 1 provides the observational evidence for an active ram‑pressure shock but does not explain why such strong stripping can occur at the galaxy's large distance where the smooth ICM would be too weak.

paper2AloneSufficient.explanation: Paper 2 discusses how local ICM inhomogeneities or motions can raise ram pressure, and mentions NGC 4522 as an example, but it lacks the specific radio‑continuum evidence that confirms the interaction is currently active.

paper1PlusQuestionSufficient.explanation: The question already supplies the observational facts, but without Paper 2 we cannot infer the need for an enhanced local ICM; the question does not state that mechanism.

paper2PlusQuestionSufficient.explanation: The question provides the observational facts, yet Paper 2 alone cannot confirm that those facts correspond to an active shock; it only offers a theoretical scenario.

questionLeakage.explanation: The question does not state the conclusion (active ram pressure + enhanced local ICM); it only lists the observations and the puzzling distance issue.

redundancyOrArtifactOnly.explanation: Paper 1 introduces the polarized ridge as an observational diagnostic, while Paper 2 contributes an independent theoretical explanation (ICM inhomogeneity) that is not merely a restatement of the same artifact.

mainVsOptionalElaboration.explanation: The central answer (active ram pressure requiring locally enhanced ICM) needs both the observational proof from Paper 1 and the theoretical justification from Paper 2; the second paper is not just background but essential for the main conclusion.

multiHopValidity.explanation: Answering the question requires (1) recognizing that the radio polarization ridge, flat spectral index and polarization gradient are signatures of an ongoing ram‑pressure‑driven shock (information provided only by Paper 1) and (2) understanding that such strong stripping at a large cluster‑centric radius can only occur if the local ICM density or relative velocity is higher than the smooth ICM model predicts, a point demonstrated by the simulations and discussion of ICM inhomogeneities in Paper 2 (which also cites NGC 4522 as a case). Neither paper alone supplies both pieces, and the question does not leak the conclusion. Therefore both papers are strictly required, making the question multihop‑valid and deserving a GOOD rating.

thinking.step1Claim: The combination of a 6 cm polarized radio continuum ridge at the eastern edge, a coincident flat radio spectral index, and a west‑to‑east increase in the degree of polarization is interpreted as the signature of a large‑scale shock caused by active ram‑pressure compression of the ISM, i.e., the galaxy is currently experiencing strong ICM interaction rather than merely showing fallback of previously stripped gas.

step1NotTrivial.explanation: Step 1 is a physical interpretation that links several observational properties to a specific dynamical mechanism (an active ram‑pressure shock). It goes beyond naming a dataset, method, or artifact and requires reasoning about magnetic field compression and cosmic‑ray acceleration.

step1LeakedByQuestion.explanation: The question lists the observations but does not provide the interpretation that they constitute evidence for an active ram‑pressure shock. The inference required in Step 1 is not stated in the question, so it is not leaked.

thinking.step2Claim: Hydrodynamical simulations (Paper B) show that, at the projected large cluster‑centric distance of NGC 4522, the smooth, static ICM density is far too low to produce the observed degree of gas stripping. Therefore, to reconcile the observed stripping (and the active ram‑pressure signature from Step 1) the local ICM must be dynamically enhanced—e.g., higher density or relative velocity due to ambient motions or inhomogeneities—providing the necessary ram pressure.

strictDependency.explanation: Step 2 relies on the conclusion from Step 1 that ram pressure is currently acting on the galaxy. Without establishing that the observed radio features are an active shock, the simulation result alone could be interpreted as evidence for a past stripping event. The inference that the ICM must be locally enhanced specifically to explain *ongoing* ram‑pressure stripping depends on the Step 1 interpretation.

entityLinking.explanation: The two steps are not merely linking the same named object (NGC 4522) across papers. Step 1 provides a physical mechanism (active shock), while Step 2 uses simulation‑based constraints on ram‑pressure strength to infer a property of the local ICM. This goes beyond simple entity tracking.

dependencyStrength.explanation: The question requires a two‑step multihop reasoning. Step 1 extracts a non‑trivial physical interpretation from the radio continuum paper, which is not given in the question. Step 2 draws on the simulation paper’s quantitative finding that the smooth ICM cannot account for the observed stripping, and combines it with the active‑ram‑pressure conclusion from Step 1 to infer that the local ICM must be dynamically enhanced. Step 2 cannot be answered correctly without the mechanism established in Step 1, and the steps are not just entity linking. Therefore the dependency is strong and the question satisfies the Dependency Strength criterion, earning a GOOD rating.

thinking.mainQuestion: Explain what the combined radio continuum observations (polarized ridge, flat spectral index, polarization gradient) together with the galaxy’s large projected distance from the cluster centre imply about the nature of the ram‑pressure interaction affecting NGC 4522 and about the physical state of the local intracluster medium.

subquestions.question: What do the 6 cm polarized radio ridge, the flat spectral index coincident with it, and the east‑to‑west polarization gradient tell us about the ram‑pressure interaction in NGC 4522?

Helicity is the only invariant of incompressible flows whose derivative is continuous in $C^1$-topology
abstract: Let $Q$ be a smooth compact orientable 3--manifold with smooth boundary $\partial Q$. Let $\mathcal{B}$ be the set of exact 2--forms $B\in\Omega^2(Q)$ such that $j_{\partial Q}^*B=0$, where $j_{\partial Q}:{\partial Q}\to Q$ is the inclusion map. The group $\mathcal{D}=\mathrm{Diff}_0(Q)$ of self-diffeomorphisms of $Q$ isotopic to the identity acts on the set $\mathcal{B}$ by $\mathcal{D}\times\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{B}$, $(h,B)\mapsto h^*B$. Let $\mathcal{B}^\circ$ be the set of 2--forms $B\in\mathcal{B}$ without zeros. We prove that every $\mathcal{D}$--invariant functional $I:\mathcal{B}^\circ\to\mathbb{R}$ having a regular and continuous derivative with respect to the $C^1$--topology can be locally (and, if $Q=M\times S^1$ with $\partial Q\ne\varnothing$, globally on the set of all 2--forms $B\in\mathcal{B}^\circ$ admitting a cross-section isotopic to $M\times\{*\}$) expressed in terms of the helicity.

First 15422 characters: Knots and links in steady solutions of the Euler equation
abstract: Given any possibly unbounded, locally finite link, we show that there exists a smooth diffeomorphism transforming this link into a set of stream (or vortex) lines of a vector field that solves the steady incompressible Euler equation in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Furthermore, the diffeomorphism can be chosen arbitrarily close to the identity in any $C^r$ norm.
Introduction: The three-dimensional incompressible Euler equation {{formula:11301c89-9c37-4dcb-8345-e33c3b620858}}describes the motion of an inviscid incompressible fluid. A steady solution of the Euler equation is a time-independent vector field {{formula:1e0146e6-afcc-4a14-ba45-0a1b4caab227}} that satisfies the above equation for some pressure function {{formula:5e55518a-2e26-4335-94a9-583b7acdfe5d}} . Equivalently, the vector field {{formula:1d30e8c3-f4cb-4796-980b-629895578334}} satisfies {{formula:4fa3ef21-9645-4ce2-8740-9f044071efb6}}where {{formula:fc3fcb34-0170-4199-89d3-6d20b254b0ac}} is the Bernoulli function. In fluid mechanics, the trajectories of the velocity field {{formula:48165c09-b29b-43d7-ba06-32c6e1e1236e}} and of its curl (i.e., the vorticity) are called stream lines and vortex lines, respectively.Since Lord Kelvin, steady solutions of the Euler equation having knotted and linked stream (or vortex) lines have attracted considerable attention, partly because of their connections with turbulence and hydrodynamic instability , . Because of the connection of the steady Euler equation with variations of the energy functional under volume-preserving diffeomorphisms, the presence of periodic trajectories of prescribed link type has also been considered to derive lower bounds for the energy functional in certain natural classes of vector fields. These bounds can actually be expressed in terms of the helicity and asymptotic linking number of a fixed vector field of the class (cf. e.g. , and references therein).Despite the large body of related literature, there are surprisingly few results of existence of steady solutions with linked stream lines, and in fact our knowledge is mostly based on numerical simulations and exact solutions. In the mid eighties, Moffatt proposed an appealing heuristic approach to the construction of steady solutions with stream lines diffeomorphic to a given link. Unfortunately, this approach requires global well-posedness for a magnetohydrodynamic system of PDEs including a Navier–Stokes equation (which, as is well known, is very far from obvious) and makes strong topological assumptions on the asymptotic behavior of the solutions as {{formula:9d3a5cef-2169-4e6b-b93a-5a58b0cab581}} .To our best knowledge, there are only two existence results of steady solutions with prescribed topological properties. Firstly, using contact topology, Etnyre and Ghrist showed that, given a certain link, there exists a (possibly incomplete) Riemannian metric in {{formula:88096924-7999-4a87-a17c-d06619b0ba45}} adapted to it such that the Euler equation in this metric admits a steady solution having this link as a set of periodic stream lines. Considering the Euler equation for arbitrary Riemannian metrics is key in order to make the problem amenable to a purely topological approach, so this method cannot be used to derive existence results for a fixed (e.g., Euclidean) metric.The second result, by Laurence and Stredulinsky , utilizes variational techniques to analyze steady solutions of the Euler equation with axial symmetry. This symmetry makes the problem effectively two-dimensional and allows to formulate it in terms of the scalar stream function. In this case, the authors prove the existence of continuous, energy-class solutions in a bounded domain with level sets of a given topological type. This approach cannot be modified to prescribe stream lines because it provides some (weak) control over the poloidal component of the velocity field but does not yield any information on its axial component. Moreover, at most the so-called torus knots could be possibly realized as stream lines of an axisymmetric solution.In this paper we aim to fill this gap by proving the existence of steady solutions in {{formula:aea820be-4b8c-4a7e-af8e-f12c137a0bcc}} with stream or vortex lines of prescribed link type. Here by a link we mean a disjoint union of tame knots, that is, of smoothly embedded circles in {{formula:5a8fecf5-79da-482a-ab39-f73991bcad5f}} . The steady solutions we construct belong to the class of (strong) Beltrami fields , i.e., they satisfy {{formula:c01103f5-f3e1-4b88-a9e9-098d0ded6079}}with {{formula:7fd8d630-b008-4116-b30b-09e7766f8a85}} being a nonzero constant. Beltrami fields also play a preponderant role in magnetohydrodynamics, where they are called force-free fields. It should be noticed that the stream lines of a Beltrami field are also vortex lines.The motivation to consider Beltrami fields to produce steady solutions with stream or vortex lines of arbitrary link type comes from Arnold's and Etnyre and Ghrist's studies of solutions to the steady incompressible Euler equation when the Bernoulli function {{formula:e96ae6fc-bfd1-48b5-8001-9ae98ef8c36b}} is analytic and nonconstant , . Under certain dynamical assumptions, these authors showed that in this case the only knots that could possibly be stream or vortex lines of a steady solution to the Euler equation in a bounded domain are those of Wada type; this result also holds in the whole {{formula:930941d1-e6da-4a41-9f42-a6038734eb91}} provided that the solution vector field satisfies the estimate {{formula:4bfa2a9e-2805-401d-96b3-22cb41dc92a9}} for some constants {{formula:4b88f7c5-6d87-4402-942b-973d09275407}} and {{formula:d94fa93a-7138-4900-89ee-13c08923da14}} . That a similar result does not hold for Beltrami fields was well known through the analysis of particular instances of ABC flows . Our main result in this paper is that actually there are no restrictions on the knot types that can be realized as stream lines of a Beltrami field:Theorem 1.1 Let {{formula:61645d68-6eff-4677-b6d0-75bb51fb7c8b}} be a possibly unbounded, locally finite link. Then for any real constant {{formula:083861d5-91eb-4188-a9aa-c3d29f0ed293}} one can transform {{formula:74e22b22-503b-4a7d-bbe7-622a6c0a15c5}} by a {{formula:d2a5fd0a-d82d-4a28-885e-2e615ed3d475}} diffeomorphism {{formula:b7e4b996-89ac-4c2f-8a38-d5bed0f3b893}} of {{formula:0433cec2-9a81-480a-970a-43810b810def}} arbitrarily close to the identity in any {{formula:26e314de-ee0d-4b70-85b6-0de7a6bb1d89}} norm, so that {{formula:250a37d0-2b5b-4a30-bc30-37f70cc4d5df}} is a set of stream lines of a Beltrami field {{formula:9fc67d1a-ce37-450f-8082-a399cf77b2c6}} , which satisfies {{formula:7c90e11b-f615-4dd4-9478-6ed81457b8e6}} in {{formula:19a580c0-f309-4c09-abe8-f83ec02a3ee5}} .The proof of this theorem is given in Section , the demonstrations of several intermediate results being postponed to Sections –. An informal guide to the proof of the theorem is presented in Section . The proof combines techniques from ordinary and partial differential equations with differential topology. While it is not easy to find parts of the proof purely relying on methods from just one of these areas, the basic philosophy is to use differential topology and ordinary differential equations (as opposed to Laurence–Stredulinsky) to gain control on the trajectories of various auxiliary vector fields, and partial differential equations to relate these auxiliary vector fields to the Beltrami equation (as opposed to Etnyre–Ghrist).Theorem REF provides a rigorous proof of Moffatt's heuristic insight that any knot should be realizable as a stream line (or vortex line) of a steady solution of the Euler equation. It also furnishes a positive answer to Etnyre and Ghrist's question of whether there exists a steady solution in {{formula:18792fb8-930f-437d-b159-271137e625f5}} having linked stream lines of all isotopy types; details and further applications will be given in Section .It should be noticed that any vector field satisfying {{formula:2925c1ee-91b8-4209-bef2-b2d8f3d36197}} has infinite energy, since in this case {{formula:e713167b-9202-4087-ada9-8c921daa236c}} and the Laplacian does not have any {{formula:976bab4d-8e9b-4b52-8e41-2173420cee09}} eigenfunctions in {{formula:10c6b45d-2761-4f7c-895f-c2b65b6629cb}} . While there are {{formula:e0ef399f-f428-4b9c-8697-4772ddd1f322}} solutions of the equation {{formula:71445bd1-5287-458e-afe1-7c03a08aa9bd}} in {{formula:7e7a0fba-dd17-47f0-9f2f-76975306d1fc}} , such as the ABC flows , the solutions given by Theorem REF are not granted to be bounded either. Incidentally, the related problem of whether there are any nonzero {{formula:0ec774fc-8788-429d-8ee3-a91a53f2f088}} steady solutions to the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equation is wide open; the fact that no bounded solutions exist either in two dimensions or in the axisymmetric case has been established recently .
Strategy of proof: Leaving technicalities aside for the moment, the strategy of the proof of the main theorem is the following. We take a connected component {{formula:d5dd8b22-6d7c-468e-a298-2f4160e73f27}} of the link {{formula:cd9c06b8-afce-48b8-8b41-08630897b226}} , which is a smooth knot, and perturb it a little if necessary to make it real analytic. We then embed the perturbed knot into an analytic two-dimensional strip and construct a vector field on this strip having the latter knot as a stable hyperbolic limit cycle. Next we extend this vector field on the strip to a local Beltrami field {{formula:2c026a37-d284-4648-82b2-3ccf9b41f80e}} , defined in a tubular neighborhood of the cycle. By construction, the field {{formula:e45e8061-7e55-42d8-9b0b-e761aa371b41}} has a periodic orbit diffeomorphic to the link component {{formula:8433394d-ae54-4f8b-b32b-024991fb4623}} , which is granted to be hyperbolic by the choice of the field on the strip and the fact that the local Beltrami field {{formula:426da9bf-56b5-4bc5-9277-64dd7ac46ac9}} is divergence-free. The above procedure is then repeated for all the components of the link. To conclude, we show that there exists a global Beltrami field {{formula:da61a652-9a75-4850-983f-4ddf882182b9}} that approximates each local field {{formula:23fc8815-6212-47a7-ba02-d849715ef212}} ; the field {{formula:197e75f6-c7db-4987-b456-d026d46695e3}} will then have a stream line diffeomorphic to each link component {{formula:c1e422f6-2851-439c-ba94-20a847965fac}} because of the robustness of the limit cycle of {{formula:19d9f785-a953-45ce-b078-48c7065d6235}} .Three main difficulties arise when trying to carry out this program. In the first place, it seems natural to define the local Beltrami field {{formula:86b9c7aa-66e2-4880-8896-1fed7f1de260}} as the solution to some Cauchy problem for the curl operator, but the fact that the symbol of {{formula:87dc5350-d863-4b17-9f10-2bb1b720291c}} is an antisymmetric matrix (and thus there are no non-characteristic surfaces of {{formula:d7e44069-13fc-4e9d-bcff-66a72b76ebf1}} ) precludes a straightforward application of the Cauchy–Kowalewski theorem. In the second place, the approximation result connecting the global Beltrami field {{formula:76acc973-7b0a-43ed-ba60-ec0eb676aecd}} and the local fields {{formula:e3177819-b084-48ae-ad50-f71d26577a7d}} should be sufficiently fine to effectively deal with the noncompactness of the link {{formula:5eed64f4-a746-403e-9405-e523ef355737}} . Thirdly and related, the vector field on the strip used as “Cauchy data” to define the local Beltrami field {{formula:89837805-fd66-413b-a3d1-df2cb5345011}} must be delicately chosen in order to ensure that the limit cycle of {{formula:da2d84ce-ca5e-4bad-8aa7-f6d423f0420f}} diffeomorphic to the link component {{formula:719b37ae-b0ac-4bf7-a085-2f91af3e6dcd}} is “robust enough” to be preserved by the latter approximation.The proof of Theorem REF , which we present in the following section, is divided into five steps. Let us very briefly comment on the purpose of each step:First of all, in Step 1 we present an abstract local existence theorem (Theorem REF ) for the equation {{formula:0de28623-ac81-463b-9dd3-a405950f4573}} with data {{formula:02bca931-1cec-4f1b-9be5-f86369860dce}} on a surface {{formula:533f66de-5d31-4ab7-a4e2-7bd34cd88254}} that will be subsequently applied to define the local Beltrami field {{formula:8d57b8c6-b4ac-46eb-a29c-6b33e14f6140}} in terms of a prescribed vector field on a strip at the link component {{formula:3bac7886-eac6-48f1-a9ee-e062ad84ccf5}} . To circumvent the lack of ellipticity of {{formula:c0b42f2f-cd66-43ac-b979-a3aea3a10a46}} (or of its counterpart {{formula:21dd79c1-9006-441d-bc09-7907cba37662}} acting on 1-forms, with {{formula:f4e7c91e-19ec-4904-966d-9f28c06bbff7}} the Hodge operator), we resort to an indirect argument with the Dirac-type operator {{formula:4fd51dd6-ae51-4083-88f1-e172b6f7ed76}} acting on the space of differential forms of mixed degrees. Here {{formula:5433a8ac-9de1-45ef-af62-b58f7a8047c6}} is the codifferential; the operator {{formula:53bbd73c-daf2-4da7-8dae-386230b54db3}} is then elliptic (thus allowing us to invoke the Cauchy–Kowalewski theorem), but it does not preserve the space of 1-forms. Ultimately, this reflects itself in the necessity of imposing some technical conditions on the vector field on the strip that will serve as Cauchy data. Appropriate Cauchy data (that is, the vector field on the strip at each link component {{formula:0ae356b0-2a76-4508-a13a-0febc73e18f0}} previously mentioned) are carefully constructed in Step 2 (Lemma REF ). Each field is required to satisfy the technical conditions demanded by the existence theorem proved in Step 1 and, besides, to have a stable hyperbolic limit cycle diffeomorphic to the link component {{formula:23dc8399-3217-461c-8d11-372b91022fbe}} . This construction is considerably simplified by the introduction of a local coordinate system adapted to the link component. The choice of Cauchy data on the strip we made in Step 2 ensures that the associated local Beltrami field {{formula:e586f7ec-53a6-49c0-9982-f91ce907332a}} obtained using the existence theorem of Step 1 also has a periodic orbit diffeomorphic to the link component {{formula:02f0cc00-0307-44d5-92d9-70af8895a74e}} . In Step 3 we show that this periodic orbit is robust under suitably small perturbations of the vector field because our choice of Cauchy data guarantees that there is a stable manifold tangent to the strip and, the field {{formula:513f58e6-779f-4994-b416-ce41a1d5413b}} being divergence-free, there must also be an unstable manifold, thereby granting that the periodic orbit is hyperbolic (Theorem REF ). In Step 4 we prove an abstract result on approximation of local Beltrami fields by global Beltrami fields (Theorem REF ) adapted to the kind of perturbations that were allowed in Step 3. This result relies on a better-than-uniform approximation theorem for the auxiliary scalar elliptic equation {{formula:2a1bceaa-7462-42b4-8139-1d24d16a1c5b}} , which in turn hinges on an iterative scheme that employs the Lax–Malgrange theorem. To conclude, in Step 5 we use the latter approximation theorem to construct a global Beltrami field {{formula:0542ccbc-8448-42db-8cd6-b22b7325c52f}} that approximates each local Beltrami field {{formula:7a01c9ef-ed81-4642-acff-668a541e6e5d}} in a neighborhood of the link com   Last 15422 characters: d-4ed0-85a7-96b9f29160dc}} and {{formula:11f93ed7-5ae6-409a-96e5-bfc91389cafb}} , which in turn implies that {{formula:63fd5ce4-262d-4015-a19f-02449cc2f150}}because, being divergence-free, the Laplacian of this field is {{formula:8514649b-bf69-4ff0-b08d-fefe4e7d9103}} . Hence the analytic vector field {{formula:d3b2a0b4-d38e-465c-ab3a-a3f1ac7c7d7f}} satisfies the Beltrami equation {{formula:d86b2b6f-8740-4fc3-9a3e-0b2daa698ed0}} and, as a consequence of the estimate (REF ), the pointwise {{formula:631e24ad-9817-4e6a-a34b-43d960f77cea}} bound {{formula:0b887a4f-312d-4cc9-8ebb-67c586f06523}}in the set {{formula:656b990d-112d-468d-bf97-78b0d164c572}} . Thus {{formula:52aa969f-8ccd-4096-8f36-eb1ac51b7aca}} is the field whose existence was claimed in the theorem, provided that the error function {{formula:d52d94fa-1879-4245-a7a9-e91c63c7fcba}} is chosen small enough (e.g., smaller than {{formula:80c6007c-795a-4ce0-96e5-e912c2a7548e}} , where {{formula:dc4d8ed6-766a-47be-a8fc-cf1566d2f6fb}} is the error function in the statement of Theorem REF ).Remark 7.2 It should be noticed that we have used that the parameter {{formula:da013cd7-07b4-42f7-a43c-c6b20835387f}} is nonzero in the last part of the proof; in fact, if {{formula:8c9a1334-4cbd-4d40-aac7-ac7bfa2f543c}} one cannot hope to approximate the local solutions by global ones because an irrotational vector field defined in a simply connected region cannot have a periodic trajectory.
Proof of Lemma : In this section we construct a vector field {{formula:b8b4cace-3fb8-469e-a342-ada2783199ce}} , tangent to a strip {{formula:ffc72b7c-52e0-44f2-b26b-acfa9a778cd1}} contained in a tubular neighborhood {{formula:012b7dd3-8f24-4a59-af5a-bded59f764b0}} of the link component {{formula:fa672fc1-a6a1-4818-84e6-a39fc8a8273c}} , which satisfies the hypotheses of the Existence Theorem REF and whose pullback to the surface has the link component as a hyperbolic limit cycle. As we will see, the 1-form {{formula:489106e2-4b9d-4c09-9ecb-01c5575d902e}} dual to the desired field {{formula:755f2576-9901-4246-8e87-93d30505b0e9}} is simply given by {{formula:66bfc6ea-beb5-486b-b436-56a68c48ffcf}} in a natural coordinate system; hence, we will start by carefully defining these coordinates on the neighborhood {{formula:d6199d58-adce-4626-b538-9301b946bbc0}} . The coordinates we shall use are {{formula:45290621-a6e6-4925-86dd-bbc3fee013ae}} , where {{formula:abbaa37d-7d8c-402f-ac4d-d56a82fc5cae}} is the signed distance to the surface {{formula:45972090-be01-4696-8cba-99e0db2b2089}} and, roughly speaking, {{formula:2209b313-a6a1-431f-823b-c22b1236518a}} and {{formula:7146c2f8-5dbc-4d01-bb55-5f66f7cfff67}} are suitable extensions of the signed distance to the link component {{formula:6b40425e-7ac5-4076-99ed-03c6806d8f2d}} as measured on the surface and of the arc-length parameter of {{formula:67c6d964-2267-4a17-a506-1218ab23955f}} , respectively.To construct the coordinates, we begin with an arc-length parametrization of the link component {{formula:9e80ee8f-b458-4c94-b4d0-465969d59c39}} , which is a periodic function {{formula:010fa1e8-2c70-4cfd-9a10-46a5c5aa6f20}} mapping the component to the reals modulo the length {{formula:a26264b0-9c2e-4007-b8f0-944b28204dd9}} of the link component (i.e., {{formula:99ceb4c4-ad31-4287-a2d5-199e8ff2d8f1}} ). By taking the strip small enough, we can safely assume that the signed distance function to the link component {{formula:ed0acaae-7071-41cb-a860-d1b2779e8b40}} , as measured along the surface {{formula:17aecd43-54fc-45c7-b71f-9331a6d5f8fb}} with respect to the metric {{formula:b6e5325a-164c-4c2f-8952-8d3d16f1bbe5}} inherited from its embedding in {{formula:d14098e3-f963-47c5-91cf-2b00f8b9d026}} , is analytic. Let us denote this function by {{formula:c69794d0-788c-4036-8b77-702fa995d3b6}} . The gradient operator associated to the metric {{formula:caa293dc-084d-40a6-8ef2-833dc9195e33}} on the strip will be denoted by {{formula:d76a66da-ab41-4bd7-a6c4-475fdd2a0205}} .We can extend the parametrization {{formula:94668497-453c-4693-8ee4-92bed6b1cd2d}} of the link component to a {{formula:e44bcdc7-7db3-4600-81bd-02a0755e3a67}} function on the surface, which we still call {{formula:62610848-0458-4d8d-82c1-b4b82d00aa4a}} with a slight abuse of notation. Calling {{formula:898d8090-38eb-452c-9d0b-0cecf8575b80}} the local flow of the gradient field {{formula:ab9edcf6-224d-4131-ba53-b0205186ef88}} in the surface {{formula:c5cf65e3-50d4-4fa1-acbd-fa17b0142ba2}} , this extension is defined by setting {{formula:81041d57-e95a-4b7e-93a5-51673cb3ffbf}}for all points {{formula:979b307c-63cd-4604-8c85-9bcd4ed4df80}} in the link component {{formula:1376523f-3e5c-4975-b2b9-dd002b5ceb31}} and all {{formula:66ad43d2-cf13-4475-845b-6420cd81c434}} for which {{formula:5e71d88d-5d28-4269-8369-963afce2452b}} is a well-defined point in the surface {{formula:d32d5633-ab2c-4b2b-90a0-7c41e9d6b288}} . By periodicity, this extension takes values in the reals modulo the length {{formula:b2d43956-b161-4c75-b644-a9dacd765b65}} . Obviously {{formula:8fb2ef1d-9378-43e4-9f50-35ec89227eca}} in the surface {{formula:518cbc1f-33cd-40b8-b61c-a7d0d3a9b97e}} , and for any point {{formula:975cd8fc-0f70-4a1c-9105-e18d92ef6b26}} there is a unique pair {{formula:ac0b08d5-df7d-4e9f-a80c-3a11715d260d}} such that {{formula:dbfc2472-aebc-4590-b4a5-a333feb06508}} (in fact, here {{formula:2db08eba-4ddb-4171-9e9d-43e5d1cbd57a}} is the signed distance {{formula:c15abbf5-c766-4a14-ba0f-16d78b07ea61}} because {{formula:2980f5c5-1bcf-46da-b890-4089358f6259}} ). Since the gradients of the functions {{formula:7c602d0a-d5a1-44de-b607-9cc294cce1ad}} and {{formula:bd0b1867-e8f4-4087-9a87-7e7bc322b023}} are orthogonal by construction, i.e., {{formula:4dc49573-722b-4a9f-ac9e-a356361560f3}}it is apparent that {{formula:0594af6c-f186-4295-8df4-cc0f9970aae3}} is a coordinate system on the surface {{formula:877f3a11-9b0e-4e84-92d9-89296346cd12}} .To construct the adapted coordinate system in the tubular neighborhood {{formula:468f1b27-9a16-40a0-904b-a2feaa4b6298}} , let us begin by considering the signed distance function to the surface {{formula:f0980c62-9bda-437e-8d94-e663f9129144}} in {{formula:374450b4-e1b6-4cae-b464-e6fc45f46e4b}} , which we denote by {{formula:3c012a1f-d311-451e-b0fd-c34d0296c145}} . This function is analytic if the neighborhood {{formula:c4cff6eb-34a4-4a45-9f3c-9a93a4e3b99e}} is small enough . We now extend the coordinate {{formula:e512b59c-51d2-4b19-91a7-7f62c5c6f3bd}} (resp. {{formula:5387bdc0-335b-40aa-947e-41bc572dc618}} ) on the surface to a {{formula:50d4d2cb-e85d-4a34-9c40-8df8c61c368a}} function mapping the neighborhood {{formula:9e1e68dc-3989-4eb7-87fb-f2eb18e67cf8}} into the reals (resp., by periodicity, the reals modulo the length {{formula:b92ef0f2-9f82-46f6-9604-ae764ed2648f}} ); for simplicity, we still denote the extended functions by {{formula:b50d1090-237d-4a24-9960-33844dde7afe}} and {{formula:6fbef5db-7cb6-4a4b-b24d-2b6db8b11f70}} . reasoning.bridgeProposition: In the Dicke model realized by a Bose-Einstein condensate in an optical cavity, the energy gap to the first excited state vanishes as the system approaches the superradiant critical point. Because cavity loss acts as a continuous quantum measurement with back action, this vanishing gap causes the diffusion rate out of the ground state to diverge, fundamentally limiting adiabatic following.
reasoning.paperBObservation: In the proposed single-atom cavity QED realization of the same Hamiltonian, the cavity field Wigner function exhibits sharp critical-type transitions—such as splitting into separated peaks—as the nonlinear coupling approaches a critical value, yet the dissipative dynamics prevent the system from reaching the pure degenerate ground state and instead yield a mixed steady state.
reasoning.appliedInference: The vanishing gap mechanism from the many-body system explains why the single-atom critical point is acutely sensitive to photon loss: as the effective Hamiltonian approaches its critical degeneracy, the system's susceptibility to cavity-induced quantum noise diverges, so the observed Wigner-function signatures are necessarily broadened or damped by dissipation.
reasoning.step1: From Paper A, we derive that the normal-mode excitation energy tends to zero at the superradiant critical point. This causes the diffusion rate due to cavity-loss-induced quantum noise to become singular, meaning the ground state cannot be adiabatically maintained and the critical point is fundamentally fragile.
reasoning.step2: Applying this to Paper B, the single-atom effective Hamiltonian also exhibits an infinite degeneracy at its critical nonlinear coupling. Consequently, the single-atom system becomes extremely sensitive to the same photon-loss mechanism: although the cavity field shows dramatic Wigner-function changes near criticality, the unavoidable dissipative mixing prevents the formation of a pure critical ground state and limits entanglement.
reasoning.connectionExplanation: Paper B identifies the critical degeneracy and acknowledges that dissipation alters the picture, but it does not explain why photon loss becomes catastrophic as the critical point is approached. Paper A supplies this by deriving a diffusion rate that diverges as the gap vanishes. Without Paper A, one might view dissipation as a small perturbation rather than a fundamental barrier. This is not entity linking or artifact reuse because the reasoning depends on applying a dynamical mechanism (gap-dependent diffusion) across two different physical realizations to interpret the nature of the steady state.

questionDraft: In the Dicke model realized by a BEC in an optical cavity, the ground state becomes fragile near the superradiant phase transition due to cavity loss. Why does this fragility arise, and how does it limit the observation of critical behavior in the corresponding single-atom cavity QED simulation of the same Hamiltonian?
question: How does the vanishing energy gap at the superradiant phase transition of a Dicke-model cavity QED system explain why photon loss prevents the observation of a pure critical ground state in the corresponding single-atom realization?
answerWithPaperReferences: In the many-body Dicke model realized with a Bose-Einstein condensate in an optical cavity [Paper A], the energy gap to the first excited state vanishes as the system approaches the critical point. Because cavity loss acts as a continuous quantum measurement with back action, this vanishing gap causes the diffusion rate out of the ground state to diverge, imposing a fundamental condition that the excitation frequency must exceed the ever-increasing diffusion rate for adiabatic following [Paper A]. The same Hamiltonian structure appears in the proposed single-atom cavity QED realization, where an effective nonlinear coupling drives the system toward a critical point with an infinite degeneracy in the cavity mode [Paper B]. Consequently, the single-atom system becomes acutely sensitive to the same photon-loss mechanism: although the cavity field Wigner function exhibits sharp transitions and peak splitting near the critical coupling [Paper B], the dissipative dynamics fundamentally prevent the system from settling into the pure degenerate ground state and instead produce a mixed steady state with damped entanglement [Paper B]. Thus, the vanishing gap explains why critical behavior in both the many-body and single-atom realizations is intrinsically fragile to cavity decay.
answerWithoutPaperReferences: In the many-body Dicke model realized with a Bose-Einstein condensate in an optical cavity, the energy gap to the first excited state vanishes as the system approaches the superradiant critical point. Because cavity loss acts as a continuous quantum measurement with back action, this vanishing gap causes the diffusion rate out of the ground state to diverge, making it impossible to adiabatically follow the ground state arbitrarily close to criticality. The same Hamiltonian structure appears in a proposed single-atom cavity QED realization, where an effective nonlinear coupling drives the system toward a critical point with an infinite degeneracy in the cavity mode. As a result, the single-atom system becomes extremely sensitive to photon loss: while the cavity field Wigner function shows sharp transitions and peak splitting near the critical coupling, the unavoidable dissipative dynamics prevent the system from reaching the pure critical ground state and instead produce a mixed steady state with limited entanglement. Therefore, the vanishing energy gap at the critical point explains why photon loss fundamentally limits the observation of ideal critical behavior in both the many-body and single-atom systems.

The Dicke model phase transition in the quantum motion of a Bose-Einstein condensate in an optical cavity
abstract: We show that the motion of a laser-driven Bose-Einstein condensate in a high-finesse optical cavity realizes the spin-boson Dicke-model. The quantum phase transition of the Dicke-model from the normal to the superradiant phase corresponds to the self-organization of atoms from the homogeneous into a periodically patterned distribution above a critical driving strength. The fragility of the ground state due to photon measurement induced back action is calculated.

First 19029 characters: Cavity QED simulation of qubit-oscillator dynamics in the ultrastrong coupling regime
abstract: We propose a quantum simulation of a two-level atom coupled to a single mode of the electromagnetic field in the ultrastrong-coupling regime based upon resonant Raman transitions in an atom interacting with a high finesse optical cavity mode. We show by numerical simulation the possibility of realizing the scheme with a single rubidium atom, in which two hyperfine ground states make up the effective two-level system, and for cavity QED parameters that should be achievable with, for example, microtoroidal whispering-gallery-mode resonators. Our system also enables simulation of a generalized model in which a nonlinear coupling between the atomic inversion and the cavity photon number occurs on an equal footing with the (ultrastrong) dipole coupling and can give rise to critical-type behavior even at the single-atom level. Our model takes account of dissipation, and we pay particular attention to observables that would be readily observable in the output from the system.
Introduction: The idea of analog quantum simulations, that is, engineering one quantum system to replicate the behaviour of another that one wishes to study, was first proposed by Feynman with regards to the infeasibility of simulating quantum systems on classical computers. The simulating system typically involves a larger number of degrees of freedom, and the effective simulation relies on precise variation of system parameters through exquisite experimental control. This idea has become reality in recent years , and fundamental models of interacting quantum systems have been realized thanks, for example, to advances in the control and manipulation of ultracold gases in optical lattices . Systems based on cavity quantum electrodynamics (cavity QED) also offer exciting possibilities, as exemplified by the recent demonstration of the Dicke quantum phase transition with a superfluid atomic gas in an optical cavity , in which a pair of discrete momentum states of the gas was used to simulate the two-level atoms of the original Dicke model of superradiance , .In this work we focus on a closely related model – the Rabi model – which describes the interaction of a two-state system (atom or qubit) with a single quantized harmonic oscillator (electromagnetic field mode) through the Hamiltonian {{formula:c9ab7b87-5c75-43f9-88c4-463cbd9f4ece}}where {{formula:64c918ed-0767-4fe6-8506-2e3ace8e3766}} and {{formula:318e9f63-3f4d-453d-ac81-c0c6fd99bd6d}} are the qubit and oscillator frequencies, respectively, {{formula:24a9a3c5-c75a-4e50-aac7-15f66161b545}} is the interaction strength, {{formula:ba4bc1aa-870e-47e1-aba5-6fe3773bd512}} are two-state operators, and {{formula:a1bad186-1edb-4f99-9213-e7748d1f279f}} ({{formula:68db425f-e92c-487c-bdc6-257ac4491509}} ) is the annihilation (creation) operator for the oscillator. This Hamiltonian predicts accurately many physical situations where an atom – artificial or real – is interacting with a confined cavity field. However, when this model is used in the description of conventional cavity QED systems, it is generally the case that the coupling constant {{formula:042c24d1-83bf-45bf-affd-7c108353e7c1}} is much (i.e., orders of magnitude) smaller than the frequencies {{formula:696ac97e-19bf-45cb-8c41-7b4eb82f819b}} and {{formula:63a31fd8-d6fb-44f7-b34c-3d158e4b534f}} . This means that terms in {{formula:27aacf42-270a-4717-b47d-e56e6091ba3b}} that do not conserve the total excitation number can be neglected, in what is known as the “rotating wave approximation.” This leads to probably the most studied model in quantum optics, the Jaynes-Cummings model : {{formula:e56a6ba4-0352-4fe7-bc9b-3917f9fc3f7d}}Recently, however, going beyond this approximation has gained newfound interest, as novel experimental systems have pushed the boundaries for the strength of the coupling between (artificial) atoms and cavity field modes. In particular, in experiments using circuit QED and semiconductor microcavities, couplings between artificial atoms and cavity modes have reached the so-called “ultrastrong” regime , , , . Here, values of {{formula:4763f2cd-b65e-478d-8801-071b8822677b}} have been realized, so that {{formula:82456f44-3468-4b07-82b0-1eabe2833618}} is no longer small compared to the mode frequency.These experimental advances have in turn stimulated new theoretical investigations (see, for example, , , , , , ), as the conventional treatment is no longer adequate. To appreciate this necessity, notice that for the Jaynes-Cummings model, {{formula:414345d0-3902-4746-8904-cf34c97b39fe}} conserves the total excitation number (i.e., {{formula:b95bb4c8-0de3-4ad6-bf94-0ab31b075524}} ), and, together with conservation of energy, this means that the spectrum is easily found. If, on the other hand, the terms {{formula:7c2462fd-ed47-4d8b-b153-463b01dd17ea}} and {{formula:6e222e79-5644-44d5-9cfa-f93aa94e44c6}} cannot be ignored, then this is no longer the case, and until recently no analytical solution was known. This was remedied in by Braak, who showed that a discrete symmetry, the conservation of parity {{formula:724f91e3-9cf3-4379-946c-6fa4ae9fc941}} , is enough for the model to be integrable and derived analytical expressions for the spectrum (see also ). Even though some intuition can be drawn from the conservation of parity , , the conventional picture of excitation exchange between the atom and the field is clearly not valid, and the spectrum of the Rabi model and the associated dynamics has been shown to exhibit a variety of novel and significant nonclassical effects, such as initial state revivals , , strong atom-field entanglement , and generation of photons from the vacuum through modulation of the coupling constant or qubit frequency , .Based on the above discussion, it follows that practical realizations of the Rabi model in the various regimes of coupling strength will be important to completing our understanding of the coupling of light to matter at the most fundamental level. We suggest that quantum simulation can be a valuable tool in this respect. Indeed, an analog simulation of the Rabi model based on light transport in waveguides was realized in , and a way of simulating the model based on circuit QED was recently proposed in . Such effective realizations are important not only because they have the potential to simulate even greater coupling strengths than can be achieved at present by “direct” coupling between two-level systems and cavity modes, but also because they offer flexible means of controlling other model parameters, as well as convenient ways of probing the dynamics through well-defined output channels and measurements.In this vein, we wish to propose a realization of the Rabi model with a single real atom coupled to a high finesse optical cavity mode. Two stable hyperfine ground states of the multilevel atom make up the effective two-level system, while (resonant) Raman transitions between them are induced by the cavity field and auxiliary laser fields. This allows us to simulate the Rabi model with essentially arbitrary tuning of the effective frequencies and coupling constant, so that any regime, including ultrastrong and deep-strong coupling, can be accessed and explored. Although the model could in principle be realized with a variety of (alkali) atoms, we focus on the D1 line of {{formula:eb6f754d-3634-4c5d-9811-269295101772}} Rb, and consider cavity QED parameters that should be achievable with, for example, microtoroidal whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) resonators .Inevitably, all such systems are subject to dissipation, and the Hamiltonian model must be expanded to an open systems treatment. We will see that our effective model is described by a master equation of the form {{formula:4bf1f648-b3c6-4789-8051-2f26a8be9f63}}where {{formula:bd9e1f83-45c0-465f-899a-76578c3221de}} is the cavity decay rate. On the one hand, we can realistically expect {{formula:ec4761cf-b7a6-460a-8c67-9f84bcf6f652}} to be small enough for the Hamiltonian dynamics to dominate on appreciable time scales, so that the Rabi model dynamics is prominent. On the other hand, the dissipative cavity QED setup provides us with a convenient means of observing the dynamics via the output field of the cavity. Furthermore, the open systems dynamics is of interest in itself, and the steady state of Eq. (REF ) is known to possess some very interesting features . It should be noted, however, that such a master equation is incorrect for circuit QED systems genuinely in the ultrastrong coupling regime , , , , as it predicts unphysical results such as photon generation from the vacuum. In our case however, such a photon flux is perfectly legitimate, given the energy input from the laser fields that help to drive the Raman transitions that we use to implement our simulation of the Rabi model. Our scheme thus offers the possibility of realizing an open systems version of the Rabi model that is subject to a simple (“conventional”) interaction with the environment (i.e., cavity damping) and can hence explore certain novel features of the Rabi model beyond what might be achievable with genuine systems.In addition, our scheme offers a generalization of the Rabi model by the addition of an extra term in the effective Hamiltonian describing a non-linear coupling between the qubit and the oscillator. This term takes the form {{formula:744776b9-bb59-4faa-b06d-905918b8a670}}where {{formula:3760c44c-6673-417d-bc54-6d5f0c82fac1}} is a tunable parameter, and can be viewed as a dynamical shift of the oscillator frequency, {{formula:6d2395f8-ce49-4b3f-8eff-599f25d7764a}} . A coupling of this nature typically arises as an approximation to the Jaynes-Cummings model in the dispersive limit (i.e., when {{formula:efc3df41-d544-4d6f-aa16-846274b30662}} ), whereas for our model it can be present independent of the relative sizes of {{formula:dcc4eddd-5c28-4e3d-b3d9-fd36126e51e9}} , {{formula:16b06cf1-f988-4dff-b818-d2efeabb4e5d}} and {{formula:c4629e45-dc44-48c3-a550-88247a950351}} , and of a magnitude that may in fact be comparable to or even larger than these parameters. Although our initial focus will be on the effective realization of the Rabi model, Eq. (REF ), such that we set {{formula:77389fbf-090a-4397-bd35-79d5bba017bd}} to zero or to a small enough value the effect of the non-linear coupling is unimportant, we will see that variation of this parameter is extremely interesting in itself and can lead to dramatic changes in the system's properties. In particular, we find two “critical” values of {{formula:5e9a5ed7-6b00-4b76-8f6b-36e572ce3f5d}} ({{formula:93cc5edc-5f24-41f7-a42d-6c96af6d274b}} ), about which, in the deep strong coupling regime ({{formula:93ae87b5-627e-4b83-bbce-235076b262eb}} ), sharp transitions occur in the quantum state of the system, marked by clear signatures in the cavity field.Finally, we would like to comment on the connection between the model proposed here, and models simulating the collective interaction of an ensemble of two-level atoms with a single field mode. Our scheme is essentially the single atom version of the proposed realization of the Dicke model presented in . By showing that an effective ultrastrong coupling regime is in principle achievable on the single atom level using a {{formula:9197ba3a-8c09-4a1f-a861-4ad896854995}} Rb coupled to a high finesse optical microcavity, we also offer a specific means of realizing the many-atom Dicke model quantum phase transition as proposed in (which requires only strong collective coupling of {{formula:5ba22305-9da5-47f3-b1df-f6f541a57d85}} atoms to a cavity mode, a much weaker requirement than the very strong single atom coupling assumed in this work). We also note the related work that has been done in .In fact, the above-mentioned experimental realization of the Dicke quantum phase transition was carried out using a scheme analogous to that of , but based upon laser-plus-cavity-mediated, resonant Raman transitions between discrete momentum states of a Bose-Einstein condensate. Notably, that particular scheme also gives rise to a nonlinear coupling term of the form {{formula:6bfb0458-4a99-4fb2-bf9c-ecef3e091a4a}} , where {{formula:f34e740c-6015-49bf-a7f7-6954e72a334d}} is the many-atom inversion operator. The Dicke model including this term has been studied theoretically in the thermodynamic limit ({{formula:4d5605cb-c19f-4f12-b592-adce09252b04}} ) in , , where phase diagrams for the semiclassical steady state have been mapped out for parameters related primarily to the experiment of . The nonlinear atom-photon coupling was shown to be of fundamental importance; in particular, a new superradiant phase is possible if the effective nonlinear coupling constant is negative ({{formula:e0b30858-9edf-48af-84c9-844c76f6c1ad}} ). Our scheme could also offer a flexible platform for exploring such a regime and, indeed, the sharp transitions we already see at the single atom level highlight this possibility.

The non-linear atom-photon interaction : In this section we continue our investigation of the effective model, Eq. (REF ), but now examine in more detail the influence of the effective parameter {{formula:24ef29c3-5160-42a6-b624-e0310b1a432d}} on the system's behavior. For small {{formula:7471be89-09ce-449d-b91f-ca3ad77f4b97}} , the dynamics is qualitatively similar to the Rabi model, as we have seen, but as {{formula:9c7ca7cd-5921-4cb6-a267-8ca73221d2e3}} grows in magnitude towards the value {{formula:e4b3f1cd-e37b-44b4-a36b-cc0013b7f064}} an instability develops in the system that gives rise to a sharp change in the system properties, particularly in the deep strong coupling regime.In Fig. REF we plot the steady state atomic inversion {{formula:cdf2215b-2749-456e-8fa8-efaff87fb149}} , intracavity photon number {{formula:b85652bd-091d-483c-aa02-7b1a78e9b7d0}} , and intensity correlation function {{formula:5dac0d48-a4e9-47ed-91b6-39e2d4cdc00f}} as a function of {{formula:0acdf15e-f9ed-4627-a193-d09f7c687b7b}} . The other parameters used are {{formula:f930cca5-a036-4186-b351-71c3d2764066}} MHz, {{formula:efe53825-ecb8-4f77-99c3-bfa2acab39c4}} MHz, and {{formula:2d13e183-afe9-459c-b609-ba227cedb5ef}} MHz. {{figure:913e3694-7052-4139-929f-a5258c8c8097}}For sufficiently large {{formula:b427cb79-4eed-4279-9e9a-ff3d5e3bc7df}} , the behavior around {{formula:8536bad6-b81b-462c-8487-6c6315017de8}} of each of the quantities plotted shows rapid and pronounced changes. (REF ), as there is an infinite degeneracy in the cavity mode at {{formula:32bda0a3-a343-44e9-900b-eb1c4013a738}} , in the sense that the energy of the states {{formula:a5aee2b6-1525-448f-be53-7b79a25034b6}} becomes independent of {{formula:45fcc522-4018-4eff-8d70-fe3d9f937a52}} . The degeneracy of the ground state and one or more excited states at a critical point is a signature of an equilibrium quantum phase transition in many-body systems, where one either has a level-crossing, or an “avoided” level-crossing that only becomes an exact degeneracy in the thermodynamic limit of an infinite number of particles . Interestingly, the degeneracy of an infinite number of states at the “critical points” {{formula:94b76e50-3621-4af4-8c93-9bf3d3384167}} that we consider here exists even for a single atom. Of course, the system we are considering is intrinsically open, and considering an equilibrium version is not necessarily meaningful, as this is fundamentally different from the {{formula:b0a1e5a2-cf8e-403e-af7d-0fd1cea48824}} limit of the dissipative model. Indeed, for {{formula:defd10d7-d6cc-4304-b437-9d1771850d72}} , the theoretical lowest energy state is one of infinite photon number and atomic state {{formula:8618a619-8535-42e3-b531-3a79c8313156}} ({{formula:3746c520-63c9-489e-a722-c209319f5a95}} ) or {{formula:2dbccc56-89dc-467a-b49d-becbb1b9960c}} ({{formula:23195441-b338-4221-8816-24d3a5c49cc7}} ). Dissipation fundamentally alters this (unphysical) picture, but signatures remain in the form of dramatic changes in the system properties.Interestingly, a semiclassical model of the system also reveals critical behaviour at the values {{formula:a247ad3f-bf34-4149-96cd-6478a2d4d49c}} .
