(REF ). By assuming factorisation of operator products, {{formula:87940ad7-cb8e-4dd8-8d45-e9b988073190}} for {{formula:67e6f8d7-dbd3-4f02-b8d7-014f703fb3cb}} and {{formula:0d95fa1c-a4de-4d4e-9f73-2822ec24ee48}} , the equations form a closed set: {{formula:869d4e7d-13f4-491b-8e97-297bf5d24097}}where {{formula:a8d63ee2-220c-4588-be19-fd50278f08d8}} , {{formula:918030ca-43d1-4284-b9fb-b15732d756c9}} and {{formula:cf9e88e9-d73a-4f07-9539-95795efa4bbf}} . Of course, this model cannot be expected to be accurate on a single atom level where quantum fluctuations are significant, but it is relevant in the thermodynamic limit of the closely related many-atom model considered in , , , . It has been studied theoretically in great detail in , where semiclassical phase-diagrams where mapped out, with distinct superradiant phases, co-existence regions and regimes with persistent oscillations. In particular, the values {{formula:5b48601b-f825-4c09-92a0-629fd1134498}} and {{formula:775ab4de-39f1-4ab1-8bee-26bf9bbc742b}} mark the change in stability of the semiclassical normal ({{formula:fe0d442c-e319-4691-b23d-8f763db01760}} , {{formula:1cd09104-a585-4c16-a1de-f7f983fbc4da}} ) and inverted ({{formula:6ef65447-dd8b-4afe-8f7e-9306c28b9ca2}} , {{formula:d37a2a77-9d45-4fec-8d69-e83e1d582cb6}} ) steady states, respectively.In fact, many of the features observed in the state of the cavity field (in terms of the Wigner function) in Fig. REF can be interpreted as manifestations on the single atom level of what become superradiant phase transitions in the thermodynamic limit: For the choice of parameters in Fig. REF , the semiclassical analysis predicts a superradiant phase for {{formula:67daa0dd-0a91-4074-96ac-c5eeac435269}} (denoted SRB in ) which on the single atom level manifests itself as a weak splitting of the Wigner-function, as seen for {{formula:bd0afc34-27ae-4f29-b39c-9e496dc6bca1}} in Fig. REF . Simulations reveal that this splitting becomes more pronounced as the number of atoms in the cavity is increased, which points to a macroscopic photon number in the thermodynamic limit. Then an extremely narrow co-existence region is predicted for {{formula:f9236c3b-cdfe-4797-983b-1f27a0b133b7}} , which we relate to the four-peaked Wigner-function for {{formula:9116de0b-8624-40ed-a65a-af887b28925d}} . In the region {{formula:951e180f-4e12-40cc-bbe4-5cd8cdfc680a}} another distinct superradiant phase comes into existence (denoted SRA in ), which in our case manifests itself as a more strongly split Wigner function. Finally, the region {{formula:66d01cf0-6e56-4c90-9896-bae517ffb3f0}} is a region of semiclassical persistent oscillations of {{formula:38d88c2c-28bf-4b24-af12-e669de6b63d5}} and {{formula:dd8003e9-29df-44e3-b95e-a64b42fa4859}} and a value for {{formula:a33eedc8-4e0a-468d-a65c-9d67cdb934eb}} that tends to zero as {{formula:112e4bcd-1cd2-4a35-91c7-0347564d8f84}} grows. This corresponds to the elongated single-peaked Wigner function for {{formula:3ee3161c-73b7-45b6-a4bf-b631b6403ab2}} in the figure. We defer a more detailed investigation of the connection between the semiclassical predictions, valid in the thermodynamic limit, and its comparison with quantum results for finite number of atoms, to a future work.The value of {{formula:96207f1f-4fad-4a7f-8f30-a79da3efe951}} also strongly influences the time-dependent behavior of the system. In Fig. REF we plot the atomic inversion and cavity photon number as a function of time, when starting from an initial state {{formula:65f4cea9-7c88-4c9f-a33a-ee5ae676c8e4}} , for five different values of {{formula:918c6b9a-8319-454f-8be6-ee8345f71406}} . We compare the effective model, Eq. (REF ), with the full {{formula:e8269a36-cd7a-474f-8f50-cd294b65622f}} Rb model, Eq. (REF ), and find excellent agreement over the timescale shown. The physical and effective parameters used are given in Table REF . The figure shows, in particular, that characteristic timescales for oscillations and decay towards a steady state vary significantly with {{formula:bab0ba14-d866-4b59-90ab-0a4b3e043d33}} , as one expects for a system exhibiting critical-type behavior and manifestly distinct phases associated with variations of this parameter. {{table:b630292f-6cab-4308-9c4e-0c51fe77dd69}}{{figure:d7678033-c898-40b7-ac1e-7a78c10fddb8}}
Conclusion: We have proposed a scheme for realizing a system with dynamics described by an effective generalized Rabi model. This scheme is based on resonant Raman transitions between stable ground states of a {{formula:7ea58e49-8c68-4cfe-a7f5-093c7a159ace}} Rb atom. By numerical solution of the master equation, including cavity decay and spontaneous emission, we have verified the feasibility of implementing this scheme, given sufficiently strong coupling of the atom to a high finesse optical cavity mode, as should be achievable with microtoroidal whispering gallery mode resonators. This scheme offers a means of performing a quantum simulation of the Rabi model with coupling strengths in both the ultrastrong ({{formula:a85e5884-def3-45af-b463-61f90eea021e}} ) and deep strong ({{formula:ac6fc8cf-cacd-4dec-ba3d-9811dfc1e018}} ) regimes, which is interesting both from a fundamental point of view and in the context of preparing highly nonclassical states.Our scheme also offers a generalization of the Rabi model, with the addition of a non-linear atom-photon coupling in the Hamiltonian that can be interpreted as a dynamical shift of the cavity mode frequency. This coupling, quantified by the parameter {{formula:7fea576f-1d0b-4588-be4b-d8df73e7995a}} , leads to fundamentally new phases of system behavior for magnitudes of {{formula:a328f481-1b39-4117-b70b-56c4691aa710}} exceeding twice the effective cavity mode frequency. Transitions between these phases are especially sharp in the deep strong coupling regime, with clear signatures in the properties of the cavity output field (i.e., in the output intensity and intensity correlation function). Extension of these results to the multiple-atom case should offer new opportunities for the study of critical phenomena in many-body cavity QED.Finally, a possibility that we have not explored in this paper, but would like to point out, is that the effective parameters in our model could easily be made time dependent. A modulation of the effective coupling constant {{formula:d0f51b3d-5fa2-4a9d-8b5a-714f132a18d1}} , for example, could be introduced by varying the laser Rabi frequencies {{formula:64ff8bad-ce51-44c5-bac2-82b55cc8499c}} (i.e., by varying the laser intensities). In the context of the Rabi model, this has been predicted to have some fascinating consequences, such as the generation of photons from the vacuum . In fact, this can be viewed as being an analog of the dynamical Casimir effect, and it would be interesting to consider how our scheme could be used to simulate this elusive phenomenon.ALG is grateful for the hospitality shown at the University of Auckland when the present paper was in progress. The authors thank Howard Carmichael for helpful discussions. ASP thanks Murray Barrett for discussions about potential level schemes in atomic rubidium.

The vanishing gap makes the system extremely sensitive to photon loss, causing a diffusion out of the ground state and preventing adiabatic following of the ground state.

In the single‑atom realization, photon loss prevents the observation of a pure critical ground state, yielding a mixed steady state with limited entanglement.
Therefore, the vanishing energy gap explains why photon loss prevents the observation of a pure critical ground state in the single‑atom realization.
